channel.title: sedzinfo · R tutorials
channel.description: Tutorials in R with the code on every page: psychometrics, adaptive testing, scale validation, statistics, machine learning and data visualisation with real data.

item.title: Multinomial Logistic Regression: How Did Federal Employees Leave in 2025?
item.description: Multinomial logistic regression in R with nnet::multinom(), on real OPM data: how about 330,000 US federal employees left their jobs in fiscal year 2025 (quit, retired, early retirement, deferred resignation, laid off, terminated), with relative risk ratios, predicted probabilities, the IIA assumption and APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Multinomial logistic regression in R with nnet::multinom(), on real OPM data: how about 330,000 US federal employees left their jobs in fiscal year 2025 (quit, retired, early retirement, deferred resignation, laid off, terminated), with relative risk ratios, predicted probabilities, the IIA assumption and APA reporting.

The question: six ways to leave

In 2025 the US federal government lost staff in several ways at once. In January, most federal employees were offered a deferred resignation: stop working, stay on the payroll until 30 September 2025, then resign. Agencies offered early retirement, carried out reductions in force (layoffs) and dismissed staff. And people kept quitting and retiring, as they do every year.

So everyone who left federal service in 2025 left in one of six ways. This page asks: among the people who left, what made one way of leaving more likely than another? Did the young quit and the old retire? Who took the deferred resignation? Who was laid off?

The outcome is a category with six values and no natural order: quitting is not “more” or “less” than being laid off. The type of outcome decides the type of regression:

Outcome Regression Example
Two categories logistic hired or not
Ordered categories ordinal logistic a performance rating from 1 to 5
Unordered categories multinomial logistic how someone left: quit, retired, laid off…

A multinomial logistic regression picks one category as the reference and fits a logistic regression of each of the other categories against it, all at the same time. The data are real: the US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) publishes a record for every federal employee who leaves.

Code 
library(nnet)         # multinom(): multinomial logistic regression (comes with R)
library(nanoparquet)  # read_parquet(): reads the Parquet files that OPM publishes
library(ggplot2)
# one colour per way of leaving, the same in every chart
exits   <- c("Quit", "Retired", "Early retirement", "Deferred resignation", "Laid off", "Terminated")
colours <- setNames(c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#eda100", "#e87ba4", "#008300"), exits)
ink     <- setNames(c("white", "white", "white", "#0b0b0b", "white", "white"), exits)  # labels on the bars
# number formats for the text
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^0", "", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
num  <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
rr   <- function(x) ifelse(x >= 100, formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ","),
                           formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2))                   # relative risk ratios

1. The data

OPM’s Federal Workforce Data has a file for every month with one row per separation: a civilian employee leaving federal service. Each row says how the person left, their age group, years of service, agency, occupation, type of appointment and more. The files are free, need no login, and come through an API as Parquet files of one to four MB.

A monthly file holds the separations processed in that month, and some of them took effect months earlier: separations of September 2025 were still arriving in 2026. So we download every file from October 2023 to the latest one, and sort the separations by the date they took effect.

Code 
options(timeout = max(300, getOption("timeout")))   # allow slow downloads
# the list of monthly files, with the current version of each
files <- jsonlite::fromJSON("https://data.opm.gov/api/v1/files/separations?current=true")
files <- files[as.integer(files$year) * 100 + as.integer(files$month) >= 202310, ]
latest <- max(as.Date(paste(files$year, files$month, "01", sep = "-")))
# the columns we need, out of the 69 in each file
columns <- c("personnel_action_effective_date_yyyymm", "separation_category", "drp_indicator",
             "age_bracket", "length_of_service_years", "supervisory_status",
             "appointment_type", "stem_occupation")
# one month: download the file and read the columns; try again if OPM asks us to slow down
read_month <- function(year, month, version) {
  url  <- sprintf("https://data.opm.gov/api/v1/files/separations/%s/%s/%s/download", year, month, version)
  path <- tempfile(fileext = ".parquet")
  for (attempt in 1:3) {
    ok <- tryCatch(download.file(url, path, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE) == 0, error = function(e) FALSE)
    if (ok) break
    Sys.sleep(10 * attempt)
  }
  if (!ok) stop("Could not download ", url)
  as.data.frame(read_parquet(path, col_select = columns))
}
raw <- do.call(rbind, Map(read_month, files$year, files$month, files$version))
nrow(raw)
[1] 808769

That is 36 monthly files, up to September 2026. The US federal fiscal year runs from October to September: fiscal year 2025 (FY2025) is October 2024 to September 2025. We keep FY2024, a year before the changes, and FY2025:

Code 
ym <- as.integer(raw$personnel_action_effective_date_yyyymm)   # e.g. 202509 = September 2025
raw$month       <- as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-01", ym %/% 100, ym %% 100))
raw$fiscal_year <- ym %/% 100 + (ym %% 100 >= 10)              # October 2024 to September 2025 = 2025
d <- subset(raw, fiscal_year %in% 2024:2025)
table(d$separation_category, d$fiscal_year)
                                    
                                       2024   2025
  OTHER SEPARATION                    16296  17123
  QUIT                                81772 159332
  REDUCTION IN FORCE (RIF)               33  10417
  RETIREMENT - EARLY OUT                206  20916
  RETIREMENT - OTHER                   3644   5249
  RETIREMENT - VOLUNTARY              55567 102490
  TERMINATION (EXPIRED APPT/OTHER)    32141  37372
  TRANSFER OUT - INDIVIDUAL TRANSFER  33003  16288
  TRANSFER OUT - MASS TRANSFER          169     84

OPM records how each separation was processed. A separate column, drp_indicator, says whether it came under the deferred resignation programme (Y):

Code 
with(subset(d, fiscal_year == 2025), table(separation_category, drp_indicator))
                                    drp_indicator
separation_category                      N     Y
  OTHER SEPARATION                   17069    54
  QUIT                               94970 64362
  REDUCTION IN FORCE (RIF)           10416     1
  RETIREMENT - EARLY OUT              8525 12391
  RETIREMENT - OTHER                  5173    76
  RETIREMENT - VOLUNTARY             69798 32692
  TERMINATION (EXPIRED APPT/OTHER)   36907   465
  TRANSFER OUT - INDIVIDUAL TRANSFER 16259    29
  TRANSFER OUT - MASS TRANSFER          83     1

On paper, most people who took the deferred resignation quit or retired. But they took a different route from people who quit or retired in the ordinary way, so we give them a category of their own. The six ways of leaving:

Way of leaving OPM category What it means
Quit QUIT Resigned
Retired RETIREMENT - VOLUNTARY, RETIREMENT - OTHER Retired on a pension
Early retirement RETIREMENT - EARLY OUT Took the agency’s offer of an early pension: age 50 with 20 years of service, or any age with 25 years
Deferred resignation any of the above with drp_indicator = Y Accepted the 2025 offer; most left on 30 September 2025
Laid off REDUCTION IN FORCE (RIF) The position was abolished
Terminated TERMINATION (EXPIRED APPT/OTHER) A temporary appointment ended, or the agency ended the employment, for example during the probationary period

We leave out transfers to another agency (those people are still federal employees) and “other separation”, which includes deaths.

Code 
exit <- c("QUIT"                             = "Quit",
          "RETIREMENT - VOLUNTARY"           = "Retired",
          "RETIREMENT - OTHER"               = "Retired",
          "RETIREMENT - EARLY OUT"           = "Early retirement",
          "REDUCTION IN FORCE (RIF)"         = "Laid off",
          "TERMINATION (EXPIRED APPT/OTHER)" = "Terminated")[d$separation_category]
exit[!is.na(exit) & d$drp_indicator %in% "Y"] <- "Deferred resignation"
d$exit <- factor(exit, levels = exits)
d <- subset(d, !is.na(exit))     # drops the transfers and the other separations

The predictors are five characteristics of each person. Years of service are cut where the rules change: the first year is usually a probationary period, early retirement needs 20 or 25 years, and a full pension needs, for example, 30 years from age 55 to 57 or 20 years at age 60.

Code 
age <- ifelse(d$age_bracket %in% c("LESS THAN 20", "20-24"), "Under 25",
       ifelse(d$age_bracket == "65 OR MORE", "65+", d$age_bracket))
d$age <- factor(age, levels = c("Under 25", "25-29", "30-34", "35-39", "40-44", "45-49",
                                "50-54", "55-59", "60-64", "65+"))
years <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(d$length_of_service_years))
years[years > 60] <- NA          # a few impossible values (up to 1,800 years of service)
d$service <- cut(years, c(-Inf, 1, 5, 10, 20, 25, 30, Inf), right = FALSE,
                 labels = c("Under 1", "1-4", "5-9", "10-19", "20-24", "25-29", "30+"))
# supervisors and managers; team leaders count as non-supervisors
supervisors  <- c("SUPERVISOR OR MANAGER", "SUPERVISOR (CSRA)", "MANAGEMENT OFFICIAL (CSRA)")
d$supervisor <- factor(ifelse(d$supervisory_status == "INVALID", NA,
                              ifelse(d$supervisory_status %in% supervisors, "Yes", "No")),
                       levels = c("No", "Yes"))
# a permanent or a temporary (nonpermanent) appointment
d$permanent <- factor(ifelse(d$appointment_type == "INVALID", NA,
                             ifelse(grepl("NONPERMANENT", d$appointment_type), "No", "Yes")),
                      levels = c("Yes", "No"))
# STEM, health or other occupations; "UNSPECIFIED" becomes NA
d$occupation <- factor(c("ALL OTHER OCCUPATIONS" = "Other", "STEM OCCUPATIONS" = "STEM",
                         "HEALTH OCCUPATIONS" = "Health")[d$stem_occupation],
                       levels = c("Other", "STEM", "Health"))
vars <- c("exit", "age", "service", "supervisor", "permanent", "occupation")
d    <- d[complete.cases(d[vars]), ]
fy25 <- subset(d, fiscal_year == 2025)
table(d$fiscal_year)

  2024   2025 
172225 329911

Each row is a separation, not a person: someone who left two temporary jobs in a year is in the data twice. We still call them people, for short.

2. Look at the data

Code 
monthly <- as.data.frame(table(month = d$month, exit = d$exit), responseName = "people")
monthly$month <- as.Date(as.character(monthly$month))
ggplot(monthly, aes(month, people, fill = exit)) +
  geom_col(width = 25) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2024-09-16"), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ exit, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  labs(title = "Federal employees leaving each month, by how they left",
       subtitle = "October 2023 to September 2025; each panel has its own scale.\nDashed line: the start of fiscal year 2025.",
       x = NULL, y = "people") +
  theme_bw()
Code 
drp_september <- sum(fy25$exit == "Deferred resignation" & fy25$month == as.Date("2025-09-01"))
# terminations of people with under five years of service, February to May
new_terminated <- with(subset(d, exit == "Terminated" & service %in% c("Under 1", "1-4") &
                                 format(month, "%m") %in% c("02", "03", "04", "05")),
                       table(fiscal_year))
new_terminated
fiscal_year
 2024  2025 
 4541 10163

In FY2024, left of the dashed line, people quit, retired or came to the end of a temporary job. Retirements peak every December, and terminations every autumn, when seasonal jobs end. FY2025 is different:

  • Deferred resignations: 106,795 took effect in September 2025 alone, when the paid leave ended.
  • Early retirements and layoffs, almost absent in FY2024, start in spring 2025.
  • Terminations of people with under five years of service rose from 4,541 in February to May 2024 to 10,163 in the same months of 2025, when agencies dismissed many employees who were still in their probationary period.
Code 
counts <- table(d$exit, d$fiscal_year)
data.frame(exit   = exits,
           FY2024 = num(as.vector(counts[, "2024"])),
           FY2025 = num(as.vector(counts[, "2025"])),
           FY2025_share = pct(as.vector(prop.table(counts[, "2025"])), 1))
                  exit FY2024  FY2025 FY2025_share
1                 Quit 81,304  93,341        28.3%
2              Retired 58,643  70,988        21.5%
3     Early retirement    206   8,523         2.6%
4 Deferred resignation      0 109,938        33.3%
5             Laid off     31  10,374         3.1%
6           Terminated 32,041  36,747        11.1%
Code 
top_exit <- names(which.max(counts[, "2025"]))

In FY2025, 329,911 people left in these six ways, 1.9 times as many as in FY2024, and the most common way to leave was the deferred resignation. From here on we use FY2025. Who left which way?

Code 
# stacked bars of shares (each bar adds up to 100%), with the larger shares labelled
stacked <- function(m, y_label, x_label) {
  ggplot(m, aes(share, group, fill = exit)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.8, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
    geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(share >= 0.07, pct(share), ""), colour = exit),
              position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5, reverse = TRUE), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colours) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = ink, guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = c(0, 0)) +
    scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
    labs(x = x_label, y = y_label, fill = NULL) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.margin = margin(5.5, 18, 5.5, 5.5)) +  # room for "100%"
    guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
}
# how the people in each group left, in FY2025
mix <- function(group, label) {
  m <- as.data.frame(prop.table(table(group = fy25[[group]], exit = fy25$exit), 1), responseName = "share")
  stacked(m, label, "share of the people in the group who left in FY2025")
}
mix("age", "age")
Code 
mix("service", "years of service")
Code 
share      <- function(group) prop.table(table(fy25[[group]], fy25$exit), 1)
by_age     <- share("age")
by_service <- share("service")
by_job     <- share("occupation")
middle     <- c("30-34", "35-39", "40-44", "45-49", "50-54", "55-59", "60-64")
  • Quitting is the usual way out up to age 45; from 50 on, people retire.
  • Early retirement happens at 50 to 59 and with 20 to 29 years of service: the eligibility rules.
  • The deferred resignation is the odd one: between 32% and 38% of the people in every age group from 30 to 64 took it, and a similar share at every length of service from one year up. Ordinary quitting and retiring each belong to one end of a career; the deferred resignation drew from all of it.
  • Layoffs hit the middle of careers: 8.7% of the people aged 45 to 49 who left, 7.6% of those with 10 to 19 years of service.
  • Terminations belong to the young and the new: 36% of the people under 25 and 35% of those with less than a year of service.
  • Occupations differ too: only 4.5% of the people in health occupations took the deferred resignation, against 45% in STEM and 34% in other occupations. Agencies could exclude positions from the offer.

Age and years of service go together, so these charts cannot tell whether age or service drives an exit. The model can: it estimates each effect holding the others constant.

3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: a reference category

Choose one way of leaving as the yardstick. We use Quit, an ordinary resignation: every other way of leaving is compared with quitting. Any category could be the reference; the predicted probabilities are the same, only the comparisons in the output change. In R the reference is the first level of the factor (levels(fy25$exit)[1] is Quit), and relevel() changes it.

Step 2: one equation for every other category

For person \(i\) and each way of leaving \(k\) other than quitting:

\[\eta_{ik} = \ln\frac{P(\text{exit}_i = k)}{P(\text{exit}_i = \text{Quit})} = \beta_{0k} + \beta_{1k}x_{1i} + \dots + \beta_{pk}x_{pi}\]

That is five equations, each with its own intercept and its own slopes. The left side is the log of the relative risk: how much more likely leaving by \(k\) is than quitting. Each equation looks like a logistic regression; the difference is that the five are estimated together, so that every person’s six probabilities add up to 1.

Step 3: from the equations to probabilities

\[P(\text{exit}_i = \text{Quit}) = \frac{1}{1 + \sum_{j} e^{\eta_{ij}}} \qquad P(\text{exit}_i = k) = \frac{e^{\eta_{ik}}}{1 + \sum_{j} e^{\eta_{ij}}}\]

The sums run over the five categories other than Quit. Each probability is between 0 and 1, and the six add up to 1. This is the softmax function, the same formula that neural networks use to classify.

Step 4: what a coefficient means

\(e^{\beta}\) is the relative risk ratio (RRR): the number by which the ratio \(P(k)/P(\text{Quit})\) is multiplied when the predictor moves from its reference level to this level, with the other predictors held constant. An RRR of 2 means twice as likely to leave by \(k\) rather than by quitting. Some books and programs call it an odds ratio; either way it compares two categories with each other, not one category with all the others.

Step 5: how R finds the β’s

By maximum likelihood: R looks for the \(\beta\)’s that make the exits that people actually took as probable as possible,

\[\ln L = \sum_i \ln P(\text{exit}_i = \text{the exit that person } i \text{ took})\]

multinom() maximises it. It fits the model as a neural network without a hidden layer, which is why it lives in the package nnet.

Step 6: count the parameters

A predictor with \(c\) categories gets \(c - 1\) coefficients: age has 10 groups (9 coefficients), service 7 (6), supervisor and appointment 2 each (1 each) and occupation 3 (2). That is 19 slopes plus an intercept, 20 per equation, and 5 equations make 100 parameters. Multinomial models grow fast: every category needs enough people for a whole set of coefficients of its own.

4. Fitting the model

Every predictor is a category, so the 329,911 people fall into a limited number of combinations of age group, service, supervisor, appointment, occupation and exit. Fitting the model to the count of people in each combination gives the same estimates as fitting the people one by one: 300 people with the same values add the same term to the log-likelihood 300 times, which is what weights = Freq does. It takes a second instead of minutes.

Code 
g <- as.data.frame(table(fy25[vars]))   # one row per combination; Freq = the number of people
g <- subset(g, Freq > 0)
nrow(g)
[1] 2416
Code 
fit <- multinom(exit ~ age + service + supervisor + permanent + occupation,
                data = g, weights = Freq, maxit = 1000, trace = FALSE, Hess = TRUE)
summary(fit)

maxit = 1000 lets the estimation run longer than the default 100 steps, trace = FALSE hides the log of the steps, and Hess = TRUE keeps what summary() needs for the standard errors.

How to read the output

Code 
s    <- summary(fit)
b    <- coef(fit)                      # one row per way of leaving, one column per term
se   <- s$standard.errors
z    <- b / se
p    <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z))             # summary() prints no p values: compute them
rrr  <- exp(b)                         # relative risk ratios
low  <- exp(b - qnorm(0.975) * se)     # their 95% confidence intervals
high <- exp(b + qnorm(0.975) * se)
Part Meaning Here
Coefficients One row per way of leaving, compared with Quit; one column per predictor level. Each number is \(b\): the change in the log relative risk Row Laid off, column supervisorYes: b = 0.40
Std. Errors The standard error of each \(b\); smaller is more precise 0.03
Residual Deviance \(-2 \ln L\): how badly the model fits; smaller is better. Used for the tests in section 6 638,895
AIC The deviance plus 2 for every parameter, for comparing models fitted to the same data 639,095
  • There are no p values. Compute them as above: \(z = b / SE\), and \(p\) from the normal distribution. For supervisorYes in the row Laid off, z = 13.43, p < .001.
  • The intercepts are the log relative risks of the reference person: under 25, less than a year of service, not a supervisor, on a permanent appointment, in an occupation that is neither STEM nor health.
  • Huge numbers, such as an RRR of 3,344 for early retirement at ages 55 to 59, mean that the reference group almost never leaves that way: nobody under 25 can retire early. They are common with categorical predictors and say little on their own; the predicted probabilities of section 5 are easier to read.
  • Every coefficient compares with Quit. supervisorYes in the row Laid off says nothing about being laid off rather than retiring. For that comparison, subtract the two rows, b(Laid off) − b(Retired), or change the reference with relevel() and fit again.

The relative risk ratios of the three predictors that are not age or service:

Code 
terms <- c(supervisorYes = "Supervisor", permanentNo = "Temporary appointment",
           occupationSTEM = "STEM occupation", occupationHealth = "Health occupation")
cell  <- function(k, t) paste0(f2(rrr[k, t]), " [", f2(low[k, t]), ", ", f2(high[k, t]), "]")
rrr_table <- data.frame(Predictor = terms,
                        sapply(rownames(b), function(k) sapply(names(terms), function(t) cell(k, t))),
                        check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
knitr::kable(rrr_table, align = "lrrrrr")
Predictor Retired Early retirement Deferred resignation Laid off Terminated
Supervisor 0.91 [0.87, 0.95] 0.73 [0.69, 0.78] 0.90 [0.87, 0.93] 1.49 [1.40, 1.57] 0.56 [0.52, 0.60]
Temporary appointment 0.16 [0.15, 0.17] 0.18 [0.14, 0.24] 0.31 [0.30, 0.32] 0.64 [0.60, 0.69] 22.39 [21.62, 23.20]
STEM occupation 1.37 [1.31, 1.42] 1.98 [1.85, 2.12] 1.87 [1.82, 1.93] 1.41 [1.33, 1.50] 1.21 [1.15, 1.26]
Health occupation 1.09 [1.03, 1.16] 1.07 [0.94, 1.21] 0.08 [0.08, 0.09] 0.98 [0.91, 1.05] 1.15 [1.09, 1.21]

Each cell is the RRR with its 95% confidence interval, against quitting:

  • Supervisors were 1.49 times as likely as non-supervisors to be laid off rather than to quit, at the same age, service, appointment and occupation.
  • Temporary appointments were 22.39 times as likely to end in a termination rather than a resignation: a temporary job usually ends by itself.
  • Health occupations had a 92% lower relative risk of the deferred resignation rather than quitting (RRR = 0.08).

The same numbers by hand

Steps 2 and 3 for one person, aged 55 to 59 with 25 to 29 years of service, and the reference level of everything else:

Code 
eta  <- b[, "(Intercept)"] + b[, "age55-59"] + b[, "service25-29"]   # step 2: one eta per way of leaving
prob <- c(Quit = 1, exp(eta)) / (1 + sum(exp(eta)))                   # step 3
round(prob, 3)
                Quit              Retired     Early retirement Deferred resignation             Laid off           Terminated 
               0.021                0.355                0.241                0.369                0.006                0.009
Code 
# new people for predict(), with the factor levels of the model
people <- function(...) {
  x <- data.frame(...)
  for (v in names(x)) x[[v]] <- factor(x[[v]], levels = levels(g[[v]]))
  x
}
someone <- people(age = "55-59", service = "25-29", supervisor = "No", permanent = "Yes", occupation = "Other")
round(predict(fit, newdata = someone, type = "probs"), 3)              # the same, from R
                Quit              Retired     Early retirement Deferred resignation             Laid off           Terminated 
               0.021                0.355                0.241                0.369                0.006                0.009

For this person the two most likely ways of leaving were Deferred resignation (37%) and Retired (35%).

5. Predicted probabilities: the easiest way to read the model

A relative risk ratio compares two exits; a predicted probability says how likely each exit is for a given kind of person. Six typical people, along a career:

Code 
career <- people(age        = c("25-29", "25-29", "35-39", "45-49", "55-59", "60-64"),
                 service    = c("1-4",   "1-4",   "10-19", "20-24", "25-29", "30+"),
                 supervisor = "No",
                 permanent  = c("Yes",   "No",    "Yes",   "Yes",   "Yes",   "Yes"),
                 occupation = "Other")
label <- c("25-29, 1-4 years", "25-29, 1-4 years, temporary", "35-39, 10-19 years",
           "45-49, 20-24 years", "55-59, 25-29 years", "60-64, 30+ years")
probs <- predict(fit, newdata = career, type = "probs")
m <- data.frame(group = factor(rep(label, ncol(probs)), levels = label),
                exit  = factor(rep(colnames(probs), each = nrow(probs)), levels = exits),
                share = as.vector(probs))
stacked(m, "age, years of service", "predicted probability of each way of leaving, FY2025")
Code 
rownames(probs) <- label
  • Early in a career (25 to 29, one to four years) people quit or took the deferred resignation: 49% and 46%.
  • The same person on a temporary appointment was most likely terminated (52%): the appointment ran out.
  • In mid-career the risk of being laid off was at its highest: 11% at 35 to 39 with 10 to 19 years of service, 9% at 45 to 49 with 20 to 24 years.
  • With 25 to 29 years of service at 55 to 59, early retirement became a real option (24%), next to an ordinary retirement (35%) and the deferred resignation (37%).
  • At 60 to 64 with 30 years or more, people mostly retired (66%).

These are probabilities for a person who left. They do not say how likely such a person was to leave at all: the data hold only the people who left.

6. Testing the predictors and the model

The likelihood-ratio test compares the deviances of two nested models. First the whole model against a model with no predictors, then each predictor: fit the model without it and see how much worse it gets.

Code 
null <- multinom(exit ~ 1, data = g, weights = Freq, trace = FALSE)
model_test <- anova(null, fit)
model_test
                                                Model Resid. df Resid. Dev   Test    Df LR stat. Pr(Chi)
1                                                   1     12075   990841.8           NA       NA      NA
2 age + service + supervisor + permanent + occupation     11980   638894.9 1 vs 2    95 351946.9       0
Code 
tests <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("age", "service", "supervisor", "permanent", "occupation"), function(v) {
  a <- anova(update(fit, as.formula(paste(". ~ . -", v))), fit)
  data.frame(predictor = v, chi_square = round(a$"LR stat."[2], 1), df = a$"   Df"[2],
             p = format.pval(a$"Pr(Chi)"[2], eps = 0.001))
}))
tests
   predictor chi_square df       p
1        age    55481.1 45 < 0.001
2    service    55065.8 30 < 0.001
3 supervisor      664.2  5 < 0.001
4  permanent    68523.4  5 < 0.001
5 occupation    15478.5 10 < 0.001
Code 
mcfadden <- 1 - deviance(fit) / deviance(null)   # McFadden's pseudo-R squared
mcfadden
[1] 0.3551999
Code 
ranked <- unname(c(age = "age", service = "years of service", supervisor = "supervisor status",
                   permanent = "appointment type", occupation = "occupation")[tests$predictor[order(-tests$chi_square)]])
  • Every predictor is significant: with 329,911 people even a tiny effect is. The \(\chi^2\) values show which predictors matter most: appointment type, age and years of service; supervisor status matters least. The degrees of freedom are the coefficients a predictor adds to all five equations: 9 age groups × 5 = 45.
  • McFadden’s pseudo-\(R^2\) = 0.36: one minus the deviance of the model divided by the deviance of the model with no predictors. It is not a share of explained variance and it runs much lower than the \(R^2\) of a linear regression; use it to compare models fitted to the same data.

How often does the model name the right exit, if it picks the most likely one for each person?

Code 
predicted <- factor(colnames(fitted(fit))[max.col(fitted(fit), ties.method = "first")], levels = exits)
accuracy  <- weighted.mean(predicted == g$exit, g$Freq)
base_rate <- max(prop.table(table(fy25$exit)))   # always guessing the most common exit
c(model = accuracy, most_common_exit = base_rate)
           model most_common_exit 
       0.5502969        0.3332353
Code 
# how each exit was classified: % of the row
round(100 * prop.table(xtabs(Freq ~ exit + predicted, data = cbind(g, predicted)), 1))
                      predicted
exit                   Quit Retired Early retirement Deferred resignation Laid off Terminated
  Quit                   57       1                0                   24        0         18
  Retired                 1      79                0                   19        0          1
  Early retirement        0      21                1                   77        0          1
  Deferred resignation   29      28                0                   39        0          5
  Laid off               35       4                0                   54        0          7
  Terminated             14       1                0                    5        0         81

The model names the right exit for 55% of the people, against 33% for always guessing the most common one. But it almost never predicts an early retirement or a layoff, even though it knows who is most at risk of them: these exits are rare, so for almost nobody are they the most likely one. Accuracy is a poor guide when some categories are rare, as Logistic Regression With a Rare Outcome shows; the predicted probabilities carry the information.

7. An assumption to check: independence of irrelevant alternatives

The model assumes that the ratio of two probabilities, for example \(P(\text{Retired}) / P(\text{Quit})\), does not depend on what other ways of leaving there are: the independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA). The textbook example: a city adds a blue bus identical to its red bus. IIA predicts that the blue bus takes passengers from cars and from the red bus in proportion; in reality it takes them almost only from the red bus.

The deferred resignation was a new way of leaving in 2025. Under IIA it drew people from the other exits in proportion. A simple check: fit the model again without it, that is without the category and without the people who took it, and compare the coefficients that remain. If IIA holds, they hardly change.

Code 
g2   <- droplevels(subset(g, exit != "Deferred resignation"))
fit2 <- update(fit, data = g2)
show <- c("age55-59", "age60-64", "service25-29", "service30+", "supervisorYes", "permanentNo")
iia  <- expand.grid(term = show, exit = rownames(coef(fit2)), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
iia$all_six   <- exp(coef(fit)[cbind(iia$exit, iia$term)])
iia$without   <- exp(coef(fit2)[cbind(iia$exit, iia$term)])
knitr::kable(data.frame(exit = iia$exit, term = iia$term, rr(iia$all_six), rr(iia$without)),
             col.names = c("Way of leaving (against Quit)", "Term", "RRR, six exits",
                           "RRR without the deferred resignation"), align = "llrr")
Way of leaving (against Quit) Term RRR, six exits RRR without the deferred resignation
Retired age55-59 104 46.59
Retired age60-64 418 372
Retired service25-29 671 1,980
Retired service30+ 830 1,632
Retired supervisorYes 0.91 1.11
Retired permanentNo 0.16 0.04
Early retirement age55-59 3,344 17,447
Early retirement age60-64 504 4,676
Early retirement service25-29 3,155 4,549
Early retirement service30+ 1,348 1,071
Early retirement supervisorYes 0.73 0.76
Early retirement permanentNo 0.18 0.08
Laid off age55-59 6.41 7.17
Laid off age60-64 4.47 6.61
Laid off service25-29 9.26 8.21
Laid off service30+ 7.35 6.03
Laid off supervisorYes 1.49 1.51
Laid off permanentNo 0.64 0.64
Terminated age55-59 1.08 1.18
Terminated age60-64 1.65 1.47
Terminated service25-29 4.60 3.58
Terminated service30+ 6.16 3.75
Terminated supervisorYes 0.56 0.54
Terminated permanentNo 22.39 21.34
Code 
moved <- function(k) median(abs(log(iia$without / iia$all_six))[iia$exit == k])   # typical change, log scale

The coefficients of retirement and early retirement move a lot: for 25 to 29 years of service, the RRR of retiring rather than quitting goes from 671 to 1,980. Those of layoffs and terminations move much less (a typical change of 12% and 11%, against 110% for retirement). So IIA is doubtful for the exits that are close to the deferred resignation. Models that relax it, the nested logit (similar exits share a “nest”) and the mixed logit, are in the package mlogit (Croissant, 2020). The formal version of this check, the Hausman–McFadden test (mlogit::hmftest()), would flag even trivial differences with this many people; the size of the changes tells more.

Three more things to keep in mind:

  • People in the same agency are not independent. Layoffs and early-retirement offers were decided agency by agency, so the standard errors above are too small. Agency as a predictor, or a multilevel multinomial model, would take this into account.
  • Only people who left. The model compares ways of leaving among the people who left; it says nothing about the people who stayed. Whether supervisors were more likely to leave at all needs the employment files too, which OPM also publishes.
  • The data keep changing. OPM calls the newest data preliminary, and late reports keep arriving: run this page again in a few months and the counts will be a little higher.

8. Reporting the results in APA style

A report (APA 7th edition) needs the outcome and its reference category, the predictors, the model test and the relative risk ratios with their uncertainty. The numbers come from the R objects, so the text below always matches the results:

Code 
n_model <- sum(g$Freq)
lr      <- model_test$"LR stat."[2]
lr_df   <- model_test$"   Df"[2]
lr_p    <- model_test$"Pr(Chi)"[2]
ci      <- function(k, t) paste0("95% CI [", f2(low[k, t]), ", ", f2(high[k, t]), "]")
# the cells of Table 1 whose p is .001 or more, for the note under it
big_p   <- which(p[, names(terms)] >= .001, arr.ind = TRUE)
p_note  <- if (nrow(big_p) == 0) "All *p* < .001." else
  paste0("All *p* < .001 except ", paste0(terms[colnames(p[, names(terms)])[big_p[, "col"]]], ", ",
         tolower(rownames(p)[big_p[, "row"]]), ": *p* ", sapply(p[, names(terms)][big_p], pval),
         collapse = "; "), ".")

Method (data analysis):

We analysed the 329,911 separations from the US federal civil service that took effect in fiscal year 2025 (October 2024 to September 2025), as recorded in the Federal Workforce Data of the U.S. Office of Personnel Management (2026), excluding transfers between agencies, other separations and records with missing predictors. The way of leaving (quit, retirement, early retirement, deferred resignation, reduction in force, termination) was analysed with a multinomial logistic regression, with quitting as the reference category and age group, years of service, supervisory status, appointment type (permanent or temporary) and occupation group (STEM, health, other) as predictors. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the nnet package (Venables & Ripley, 2002).

Results:

The predictors improved the fit over an intercept-only model, χ²(95) = 351,947, p < .001, McFadden’s R² = .36. Holding the other predictors constant, supervisors were more likely than non-supervisors to be laid off rather than to quit, RRR = 1.49, 95% CI [1.40, 1.57], employees on temporary appointments were more likely to be terminated rather than to quit, RRR = 22.39, 95% CI [21.62, 23.20], and employees in health occupations were less likely to take the deferred resignation rather than to quit, RRR = 0.08, 95% CI [0.08, 0.09] (Table 1). Compared with employees with less than a year of service, those with 25 to 29 years were more likely to take the deferred resignation rather than to quit, RRR = 33.93, 95% CI [30.72, 37.48].

Table 1

Relative Risk Ratios From a Multinomial Logistic Regression of the Way of Leaving Federal Service, FY2025

Predictor Retired Early retirement Deferred resignation Laid off Terminated
Supervisor 0.91 [0.87, 0.95] 0.73 [0.69, 0.78] 0.90 [0.87, 0.93] 1.49 [1.40, 1.57] 0.56 [0.52, 0.60]
Temporary appointment 0.16 [0.15, 0.17] 0.18 [0.14, 0.24] 0.31 [0.30, 0.32] 0.64 [0.60, 0.69] 22.39 [21.62, 23.20]
STEM occupation 1.37 [1.31, 1.42] 1.98 [1.85, 2.12] 1.87 [1.82, 1.93] 1.41 [1.33, 1.50] 1.21 [1.15, 1.26]
Health occupation 1.09 [1.03, 1.16] 1.07 [0.94, 1.21] 0.08 [0.08, 0.09] 0.98 [0.91, 1.05] 1.15 [1.09, 1.21]

Note. N = 329,911. Reference category: quit. Each cell is the relative risk ratio [95% confidence interval] of leaving in the way named in the column rather than quitting. The model also includes age group and years of service. All p < .001 except Health occupation, retired: p = .003; Health occupation, early retirement: p = .305; Health occupation, laid off: p = .518.

Points to remember:

  • Name the reference category: every coefficient compares with it.
  • Report relative risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and say that they hold the other predictors constant.
  • Give the model test (\(\chi^2\) with its degrees of freedom) and a pseudo-\(R^2\), and say which one.
  • With hundreds of thousands of people every p is tiny: report the size of the effects, and predicted probabilities where they help.
  • Say which categories you merged or left out, and why.
  • Cite R and the packages; citation("nnet") gives the reference.

9. Summary

When The outcome is a category with three or more values and no order
Why not separate logistic regressions Their probabilities do not add up to 1, and there is no single test of a predictor
Why not ordinal logistic regression The categories have no order
How (R) nnet::multinom(y ~ x, data); with counts per combination of values, weights = n
Output One equation per category against the reference; exp() of a coefficient is a relative risk ratio
Easiest to read Predicted probabilities: predict(fit, newdata, type = "probs")
Tests Likelihood-ratio tests with anova(); McFadden’s pseudo-\(R^2\)
Assumptions Independent observations; independence of irrelevant alternatives; enough people in every category for its own set of coefficients
If IIA fails A nested or mixed logit, with mlogit

References

Agresti, A. (2013). Categorical data analysis (3rd ed.). Wiley.

Croissant, Y. (2020). Estimation of random utility models in R: The mlogit package. Journal of Statistical Software, 95(11), 1–41. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v095.i11

Csárdi, G., & Mühleisen, H. (2026). nanoparquet: Read and write ‘Parquet’ files (R package version 0.5.2). https://github.com/r-lib/nanoparquet

Hausman, J., & McFadden, D. (1984). Specification tests for the multinomial logit model. Econometrica, 52(5), 1219–1240.

McFadden, D. (1974). Conditional logit analysis of qualitative choice behavior. In P. Zarembka (Ed.), Frontiers in econometrics (pp. 105–142). Academic Press.

U.S. Office of Personnel Management. (2026). Federal Workforce Data: Separations [Data set]. https://data.opm.gov/

Venables, W. N., & Ripley, B. D. (2002). Modern applied statistics with S (4th ed.). Springer.

This post first appeared on Worked Examples in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Fired for AI, Hired Back: What Happens When Companies Replace Workers with AI
item.description: Job cuts blamed on AI, the US layoff and hiring rates, how many laid-off workers are hired back and how fast, what it costs, and the cases of Klarna, Commonwealth Bank and Ford, in Challenger, JOLTS, Visier and survey data.
item.content:encoded:
Job cuts blamed on AI, the US layoff and hiring rates, how many laid-off workers are hired back and how fast, what it costs, and the cases of Klarna, Commonwealth Bank and Ford, in Challenger, JOLTS, Visier and survey data.

What is this?

Since ChatGPT came out at the end of 2022, more and more companies have said that they are cutting jobs because of artificial intelligence, and some of them have later had to hire people back. This page puts together the data there are on what happens then:

  1. How many jobs are cut “because of AI”?
  2. Does the labour market show a wave of AI layoffs?
  3. How many of the people laid off are hired back, and how fast?
  4. Does it save money?
  5. What happened at Klarna, Commonwealth Bank of Australia and Ford?
  6. What do employers and analysts say?
  7. Why does it happen, and what can a company do instead?

The data are of four kinds, and they are not equally solid:

  • Counts of what happened: the layoffs and hires of the whole US economy, from the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) of the Bureau of Labor Statistics, downloaded from FRED when the document is knitted; and the records of 2.4 million employees, in which Visier counted how many of the people laid off were hired back by the same employer.
  • Counts of what companies said: the job cuts announced by US employers, with the reason they gave, counted by the outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.
  • Surveys of HR professionals and business leaders: Careerminds, Orgvue and Gartner.
  • Forecasts of analysts: Forrester and Gartner.

Challenger, Visier and the surveys publish their figures in press releases and reports, not as datasets, so the figures are typed in below, and the page each one comes from is listed under Sources.

What these numbers can and cannot say. No source counts the people who were replaced by AI and then hired back. Challenger counts the reason a company gives for a cut, and “AI” may sound better to investors than “weak sales”. Visier counts people hired back after any layoff, not only after cuts blamed on AI. The surveys ask the people who made the decisions, and the firms that run them sell outplacement, people analytics or workforce planning. Together they show the size of what is happening and its direction, not exact numbers, and almost all of them are about the United States.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages("plotly")
library(plotly)

The data

Code 
# a FRED series as dates and values; FRED leaves the months without a value empty
fred <- function(id) {
  url <- paste0("https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=", id)
  x <- tryCatch(read.csv(url),
                error = function(e) stop("Could not download ", id, " from FRED: ", conditionMessage(e), call. = FALSE))
  names(x) <- c("date", "value")
  x$date <- as.Date(x$date)
  x$value <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x$value))
  x[!is.na(x$value), ]
}
# JOLTS, all US non-farm employers, seasonally adjusted, monthly: layoffs and discharges and hires as
# % of employment, and layoffs and discharges in thousands
layoffs_rate <- fred("JTSLDR")
hires_rate <- fred("JTSHIR")
layoffs <- fred("JTSLDL")
# job cuts announced by US employers, for all reasons and those for which the employer cited
# artificial intelligence; Challenger started counting AI as a reason in 2023. The AI cuts of 2024
# are not published on their own: they are the 71,825 AI cuts from 2023 to 2025 minus those of 2023
# and of 2025
challenger <- data.frame(
  period = c("2023", "2024", "2025", "2026, Jan-Oct"),
  from = as.Date(c("2023-01-01", "2024-01-01", "2025-01-01", "2026-01-01")),
  to = as.Date(c("2023-12-01", "2024-12-01", "2025-12-01", "2026-10-01")),
  ai = c(4247, 71825 - 4247 - 54836, 54836, 121401),
  all = c(721677, 761358, 1206374, 617189)
)
challenger$months <- 12 * (as.numeric(format(challenger$to, "%Y")) - as.numeric(format(challenger$from, "%Y"))) +
  as.numeric(format(challenger$to, "%m")) - as.numeric(format(challenger$from, "%m")) + 1
# the AI cuts of 2026 from the start of the year to the end of each month; the cuts of a month are the
# difference between two months
ai_2026 <- data.frame(
  month = seq(as.Date("2026-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = 10),
  to_date = c(7624, 12304, 27645, 49135, 87714, 101743, 112713, 116175, 120136, 121401)
)
ai_2026$cuts <- diff(c(0, ai_2026$to_date))
# Visier: rehiring by the same employer after a layoff, in the records of 2.4 million employees of 142
# organisations (actual records, not a survey)
visier <- list(rehired = 5.3, months = "just under six", pay_back = 5, pay_stayed = 2,
               high_performers = 120, managers = 68)
# Careerminds: 600 HR professionals whose organisations made layoffs in the 12 months before
# February 2026. The share of the roles that were cut and then filled again, the time until they
# were filled again, and the money the layoffs saved after the rehiring, % of the HR professionals
roles_back <- data.frame(
  answer = c("The rest: under a quarter, or none", "A quarter to a half", "More than half"),
  share = c(100 - 32.7 - 35.6, 32.7, 35.6)
)
time_back <- data.frame(
  answer = c("Under 3 months", "3 to 6 months", "6 to 12 months", "Over 12 months"),
  share = c(17.8, 52.1, 27.8, 2.1)
)
money <- data.frame(
  answer = c("Rehiring cost more than the layoffs saved", "Broke even", "Came out ahead"),
  share = c(30.9, 42.37, 26.69)
)
careerminds <- list(lost_skills = 32.9, oversight = 54.6, fully_replaced = 21.4, some_replaced = 66.1,
                    worse = 12.3, repeat_unchanged = 8.4, never_discussed = 55.1,
                    redeploy_quarter = 51.3, redeploy_half = 28.3, ai_understanding = 53.8, skills_data = 40.6)
Code 
red <- "#d62728"
blue <- "#1f77b4"
gray <- "#9e9e9e"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b"   # also the color of the notes and the labels
# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(p, title, source, y_title = "", y_axis = list(), x_axis = list(), annotations = list(),
                  margin = list(t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.16, ...) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source), xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 0, y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = modifyList(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = modifyList(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) %>% config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
# the answers to one survey question as horizontal bars, the first answer at the top, with the share
# at the end of each bar; color is one color, or one per answer
answers <- function(x, title, source, color = blue) {
  x$answer <- factor(x$answer, levels = rev(x$answer))
  plot_ly(x,
    x = ~share, y = ~answer, type = "bar", orientation = "h", marker = list(color = color),
    text = ~paste0(format(round(share, 1), nsmall = 1), "%"), textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
    textfont = list(color = dark_gray), hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f}%<extra></extra>"
  ) %>%
    chart(title, source, x_axis = list(ticksuffix = "%", range = c(0, max(x$share) * 1.2)),
          margin = list(l = 10, t = 70, b = 80), note_y = -0.25, bargap = 0.35) %>%
    layout(yaxis = list(automargin = TRUE))
}
# short labels of numbers
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1)
thousands <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
month_year <- function(d) format(d, "%B %Y")

1. How many jobs are cut “because of AI”?

Code 
challenger$share <- 100 * challenger$ai / challenger$all
peak <- ai_2026[which.max(ai_2026$cuts), ]
last <- ai_2026[nrow(ai_2026), ]

More every year, from almost nothing. In 2023, the first year that Challenger counted it, US employers cited AI for 4,247 job cuts, 0.6% of all the cuts they announced. In 2025 they cited it for 54,836, 4.5% of all cuts, and in the first ten months of 2026 for 121,401, 20%: more than in the three years before put together. In the spring of 2026 AI was the reason that employers cited most often.

Code 
plot_ly(challenger,
  x = ~factor(period, levels = period), y = ~ai, type = "bar", marker = list(color = blue),
  text = ~paste0(thousands(ai), "<br>", percent(share, 1), " of all cuts"), textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE, textfont = list(color = dark_gray),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:,} job cuts<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart("Job cuts for which US employers cited AI", "Challenger, Gray & Christmas, job cuts reports",
        y_axis = list(range = c(0, max(challenger$ai) * 1.25), tickformat = ","), bargap = 0.45)

Interactive chart: Job cuts for which US employers cited AI

But not a steady rise. The AI cuts of 2026 came in a few large announcements: 38,579 in May 2026, the most of any month since Challenger started counting, then fewer every month, down to 1,265 in October 2026.

Code 
plot_ly(ai_2026,
  x = ~month, y = ~cuts, type = "bar", marker = list(color = blue),
  hovertemplate = "%{x|%B %Y}: %{y:,} job cuts<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart("AI-cited job cuts by month, 2026", "Challenger, Gray & Christmas, job cuts reports",
        y_axis = list(tickformat = ","), x_axis = list(tickformat = "%b", dtick = "M1"), bargap = 0.3)

Interactive chart: AI-cited job cuts by month, 2026

These are announcements and reasons given, not people who lost their job because a machine now does it. An announced cut can take months or years, or never happen, and a company that cuts jobs to save money can choose to say that AI made it possible. A Gartner analyst, Kathy Ross, said that most recent reductions “were influenced by broader economic conditions rather than automation alone”.

2. Does the labour market show a wave of AI layoffs?

Code 
latest_layoffs <- layoffs_rate[nrow(layoffs_rate), ]
latest_hires <- hires_rate[nrow(hires_rate), ]
before <- function(x) mean(x$value[x$date >= as.Date("2015-01-01") & x$date <= as.Date("2019-12-01")])
peak_layoffs <- layoffs_rate[which.max(layoffs_rate$value), ]

No. If companies were replacing many workers with AI, more people would lose their jobs. JOLTS counts every layoff and discharge in the US every month, and since ChatGPT came out the share of workers laid off or discharged in a month has stayed at about 1%: 1.0% in September 2026, against 1.2% on average in 2015 to 2019, before COVID-19. A real wave of layoffs looks like March 2020, when 8.6% of all workers were laid off in one month.

What has changed is hiring: 3.4% of workers were hired in September 2026, against 3.8% in 2015 to 2019. Companies are not firing more people; they are taking on fewer. A hiring freeze is also the quietest way to replace people with AI: no one is laid off, the people who leave are not replaced, and the work that they did goes to the software or to the people who stay.

Code 
chatgpt <- as.Date("2022-11-30")
plot_ly() %>%
  add_lines(data = hires_rate, x = ~date, y = ~value, name = "Hires", line = list(color = blue, width = 2),
            hovertemplate = "%{x|%B %Y}: %{y:.1f}% of employment<extra>Hires</extra>") %>%
  add_lines(data = layoffs_rate, x = ~date, y = ~value, name = "Layoffs and discharges", line = list(color = red, width = 2),
            hovertemplate = "%{x|%B %Y}: %{y:.1f}% of employment<extra>Layoffs and discharges</extra>") %>%
  chart("US hires and layoffs in a month, % of employment", "US Bureau of Labor Statistics, JOLTS, via FRED (JTSHIR, JTSLDR)",
        y_axis = list(ticksuffix = "%", rangemode = "tozero"), legend = legend_top,
        shapes = list(list(type = "line", x0 = chatgpt, x1 = chatgpt, y0 = 0, y1 = 1, yref = "paper",
                           line = list(color = dark_gray, width = 1, dash = "dot"))),
        annotations = list(list(x = chatgpt, y = 1, yref = "paper", text = "ChatGPT", xanchor = "right", yanchor = "top",
                                xshift = -4, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = dark_gray))))

Interactive chart: US hires and layoffs in a month, % of employment

AI-cited cuts are a small part of all layoffs. Even in 2026, the job cuts for which employers cited AI were less than 1% of the people laid off or discharged in the US. The comparison is rough, as Challenger counts announcements and JOLTS counts people who left, and JOLTS also counts people fired for their work, but the difference is of a hundred times or more.

Code 
# the AI cuts per month against the layoffs and discharges per month, over the months of each period
# that JOLTS has published
challenger$layoffs <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(challenger)), function(i) {
  1000 * mean(layoffs$value[layoffs$date >= challenger$from[i] & layoffs$date <= challenger$to[i]])
})
challenger$of_layoffs <- 100 * (challenger$ai / challenger$months) / challenger$layoffs
plot_ly(challenger,
  x = ~factor(period, levels = period), y = ~of_layoffs, type = "bar", marker = list(color = blue),
  text = ~percent(of_layoffs, 2), textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE, textfont = list(color = dark_gray),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.2f}%<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart("Job cuts citing AI, % of all layoffs and discharges in the US", "Challenger, Gray & Christmas; BLS, JOLTS, via FRED (JTSLDL)",
        y_axis = list(ticksuffix = "%", range = c(0, max(challenger$of_layoffs) * 1.25)), bargap = 0.45)

Interactive chart: Job cuts citing AI, % of all layoffs and discharges in the US

3. How many are hired back, and how fast?

“Hired back” means two different things, and the data on them are very different:

  • The same person comes back. In the records of 2.4 million employees, Visier found that about 5.3% of the people laid off were later hired again by the employer that laid them off, after just under six months on average. This is after any layoff, not only those blamed on AI. The people who come back are not a random group: high performers were rehired 120% more often than others, and managers 68% more often than employees who manage no one. The company calls back the people it most needs.
  • The job is filled again, by the same person or by someone else, perhaps with another title, at a lower wage, through an agency or in another country. This is what the surveys ask about, and it is much more common. Of 600 HR professionals whose organisations had made layoffs in the previous year, 35.6% said that their organisation had filled again more than half of the roles it cut, and 32.7% between a quarter and a half.
Code 
answers(roles_back, "Roles cut and then filled again, % of HR professionals", "Careerminds, survey of 600 HR professionals, February 2026")

Interactive chart: Roles cut and then filled again, % of HR professionals

And fast. Of the organisations that filled the roles again, 69.9% did so within six months of the cuts, 17.8% within three.

Code 
answers(time_back, "Time until the roles were filled again, % of HR professionals", "Careerminds, survey of 600 HR professionals, February 2026")

Interactive chart: Time until the roles were filled again, % of HR professionals

4. Does it save money?

For most, it did not. Asked what the layoffs saved once the roles had been filled again, 30.9% of the HR professionals said that the rehiring cost more than the layoffs saved, and 42.4% that they broke even. Only 26.7% came out ahead.

Code 
answers(money, "Savings after the rehiring, % of HR professionals",
        "Careerminds, survey of 600 HR professionals, February 2026", color = c(red, gray, blue))

Interactive chart: Savings after the rehiring, % of HR professionals

The reason is simple arithmetic. Cutting a job saves its pay for every month that it stays empty, but the cut and the rehiring cost money once: the severance pay, the recruiting and the onboarding, the months before the new person does the job well, and, for people who come back, a higher wage. Visier found that the people hired back got a pay rise of 5%, against 2% for those who had stayed. If the job is filled again soon, the months of pay saved do not cover these costs.

The model below makes that concrete. Its numbers are assumptions, not data: every cost is in months of the pay of the job that is cut, so that it fits any job and any country. Change them to fit a real case.

Code 
severance <- 2           # months of pay paid when the job is cut; depends on the country and the years of service
hiring <- 1              # recruiting, interviews and onboarding when the job is filled again
ramp_up <- 3 * 0.5       # the new person does half the work in the first 3 months
premium <- 12 * 0.05     # a 5% higher wage for a year, the rise that Visier found for people hired back
ai_cost <- 0.10          # what the AI costs per month, as a share of the pay that the cut saves
one_off <- severance + hiring + ramp_up + premium
saving <- data.frame(months = 0:24)
saving$net <- saving$months * (1 - ai_cost) - one_off
break_even <- one_off / (1 - ai_cost)

With these assumptions the cut costs 5.1 months of pay once, and saves 0.9 of a month’s pay for every month that the job stays empty. A job filled again in less than 5.7 months costs more than it saves, and the shaded area shows that, in the Careerminds survey, 70% of the roles were filled again in the first six months.

Code 
plot_ly(saving,
  x = ~months, y = ~net, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = blue, width = 2),
  hovertemplate = "Filled again after %{x} months: %{y:.1f} months of pay<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart("What a job cut saves, by the months until the job is filled again", "the assumptions of the model above",
        y_title = "Months of pay saved (net)", x_axis = list(title = "Months until the job is filled again", dtick = 3),
        y_axis = list(zeroline = TRUE, zerolinecolor = dark_gray),
        shapes = list(list(type = "rect", x0 = 0, x1 = 6, y0 = 0, y1 = 1, yref = "paper",
                           fillcolor = gray, opacity = 0.15, line = list(width = 0))),
        annotations = list(
          list(x = 3, y = 1, yref = "paper", text = paste0("Filled again within 6 months:<br>",
                                                           percent(time_back$share[1] + time_back$share[2]), " of the roles"),
               yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)),
          list(x = break_even, y = 0, text = paste("Break-even:", one(break_even), "months"), ax = 70, ay = 35, xanchor = "left",
               arrowcolor = dark_gray, font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray))),
        margin = list(t = 70, b = 110), note_y = -0.3)

Interactive chart: What a job cut saves, by the months until the job is filled again

The model leaves out the costs that are hardest to count, and the next section shows that they can be the larger part: service that gets worse, overtime for the people who stayed, and knowledge that left with the people who were let go. In the Careerminds survey, 32.9% said that their organisation lost critical skills and expertise with the layoffs. It also leaves out the cheaper ways of filling a job again, with lower pay or in another country, which make the cut save more.

5. Three cases

Code 
cases <- data.frame(
  Company = c("Klarna (payments, Sweden)", "Commonwealth Bank of Australia", "Ford (cars, US)"),
  `What it did` = c(
    "Stopped hiring anyone but engineers in December 2023. In February 2024 it said that its AI assistant was doing the work of 700 full-time customer service agents, most of whom worked for outside providers. Its staff fell from 5,441 in 2022 to 4,201 in 2023.",
    "In July 2025 it told the union that 45 customer service jobs were no longer needed, because a new AI voice bot had reduced the calls.",
    "Relied \"more and more on automated quality systems\" to find faults in its cars."
  ),
  `What happened` = c(
    "In May 2025 its CEO said that cost had been \"a too predominant evaluation factor\" and the result was \"lower quality\". Klarna started hiring people for customer service again, and now says that human service will be \"a VIP thing\", while AI answers the simple questions.",
    "The union said that the calls had in fact increased, and that the staff were doing overtime and team leaders were answering phones. It took the case to the Fair Work Commission. In August 2025 the bank said that it had been wrong, apologised, and kept the jobs.",
    "In June 2026 it said that it had hired 350 veteran engineers, some of them former Ford employees and others from its suppliers, to find faults before parts reach the plant, to train younger engineers and to reprogram its AI tools. Ford keeps using AI."
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(cases, caption = "Companies that replaced people with AI and then needed people again")
Companies that replaced people with AI and then needed people again
Company What it did What happened
Klarna (payments, Sweden) Stopped hiring anyone but engineers in December 2023. In February 2024 it said that its AI assistant was doing the work of 700 full-time customer service agents, most of whom worked for outside providers. Its staff fell from 5,441 in 2022 to 4,201 in 2023. In May 2025 its CEO said that cost had been “a too predominant evaluation factor” and the result was “lower quality”. Klarna started hiring people for customer service again, and now says that human service will be “a VIP thing”, while AI answers the simple questions.
Commonwealth Bank of Australia In July 2025 it told the union that 45 customer service jobs were no longer needed, because a new AI voice bot had reduced the calls. The union said that the calls had in fact increased, and that the staff were doing overtime and team leaders were answering phones. It took the case to the Fair Work Commission. In August 2025 the bank said that it had been wrong, apologised, and kept the jobs.
Ford (cars, US) Relied “more and more on automated quality systems” to find faults in its cars. In June 2026 it said that it had hired 350 veteran engineers, some of them former Ford employees and others from its suppliers, to find faults before parts reach the plant, to train younger engineers and to reprogram its AI tools. Ford keeps using AI.

The three cases are different from each other, and each is different from the headline “fired for AI, hired back”:

  • Klarna did not fire 700 people: most of its customer service agents worked for outside providers, and the company shrank mainly by not hiring. What failed was the quality of the service, and the CEO said so.
  • Commonwealth Bank measured the wrong thing. The bot answered some calls, but the work did not go away: it went to the people who stayed.
  • Ford did not say that it had laid these engineers off because of AI. Its case is about knowledge: the experience of veteran engineers was not in the data from which its automated systems learned, and Ford needed people who had it.

6. What do employers and analysts say?

Code 
surveys <- data.frame(
  Source = c("Orgvue", "Careerminds", "Gartner", "Gartner", "Forrester"),
  Date = c("April 2025", "February 2026", "October 2025", "March 2026", "November 2025"),
  Kind = c("Survey", "Survey", "Survey", "Forecast", "Forecast"),
  `Who` = c("More than 1,000 business leaders", "600 HR professionals", "321 customer service and support leaders",
            "Analysts", "Analysts"),
  Finding = c(
    "39% made people redundant because of AI, and 55% of these say that they made the wrong decisions: about one in five of all.",
    paste0("Only ", careerminds$repeat_unchanged, "% would make the same AI-driven layoffs again without changes."),
    "Only about 20% had reduced their number of customer service agents because of AI; most kept them stable.",
    "By 2027, 50% of the companies that attributed a cut in headcount to AI will rehire staff to \"perform similar functions, but under different job titles\".",
    "\"Half of AI-attributed layoffs\" will be \"quietly reversed, with jobs returning offshore or at lower wages\"."
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(surveys, caption = "Surveys of employers and forecasts of analysts")
Surveys of employers and forecasts of analysts
Source Date Kind Who Finding
Orgvue April 2025 Survey More than 1,000 business leaders 39% made people redundant because of AI, and 55% of these say that they made the wrong decisions: about one in five of all.
Careerminds February 2026 Survey 600 HR professionals Only 8.4% would make the same AI-driven layoffs again without changes.
Gartner October 2025 Survey 321 customer service and support leaders Only about 20% had reduced their number of customer service agents because of AI; most kept them stable.
Gartner March 2026 Forecast Analysts By 2027, 50% of the companies that attributed a cut in headcount to AI will rehire staff to “perform similar functions, but under different job titles”.
Forrester November 2025 Forecast Analysts “Half of AI-attributed layoffs” will be “quietly reversed, with jobs returning offshore or at lower wages”.

The surveys agree on the direction: many of the companies that cut jobs for AI regret it, and many fill the jobs again. The two forecasts agree on what happens next: the jobs come back in another form, with other titles, at lower pay or in another country. Neither form shows up as a company “hiring back the people it replaced”, which is one reason why the counts of rehiring are low and the counts of roles filled again are high.

7. Why does it happen, and what can a company do instead?

Why it happens:

  1. AI does tasks, but companies cut jobs. Almost every job has a part that AI does well and a part that it does not. In the Careerminds survey, only 21.4% said that AI fully replaced the roles with no problems; 66.1% said that it replaced some of them, and 54.6% that the layoffs were not worth it because of the human oversight the AI needed.
  2. Decisions are made on promises, not on results. 53.8% said that they would have decided better with a clearer understanding of what AI could do.
  3. Cost is measured, quality is not. Klarna’s CEO said so in as many words, and Commonwealth Bank counted the calls that the bot answered, not the work that was left.
  4. Knowledge that is not written down leaves with the people. AI learns from the data it is given, and the experience of people who know the exceptions, the customers and the history is rarely in those data. This is what Ford found.
  5. “AI” is sometimes only the label. A cut made to save money can be announced as a cut made possible by AI, and the work comes back when it turns out that someone still has to do it.

What a company can do instead:

  1. Split each job into tasks before cutting jobs, and cut only where AI can do the whole job, or join the parts that remain into new jobs.
  2. Run the AI next to the people first, for long enough, and measure quality, mistakes, the work that is left and customer satisfaction, not only cost and speed.
  3. Move people instead of letting them go. 55.1% of the HR professionals said that moving people to other roles was never formally discussed, and 51.3% that up to a quarter of the roles cut could have been redeployed (28.3% said a quarter to a half). Knowing the skills of the people who are already there makes this possible: 40.6% said that they would have needed more data on skills.
  4. Keep the knowledge: write down how the work is done, and keep a core of experienced people who can train others and correct the AI.
  5. If people must go, let them go well. The people a company most often hires back are its high performers and managers, and they come back only if they left on good terms.

So, what happens?

  1. More and more job cuts are blamed on AI: 121,401 in the first ten months of 2026, 20% of all job cuts announced in the US, against 4,247 in all of 2023.
  2. But there is no wave of layoffs: the share of US workers laid off in a month is still about 1%, as before ChatGPT, and AI-cited cuts are less than 1% of all layoffs. What has fallen is hiring.
  3. The same people rarely come back, about 5.3% of those laid off, but the jobs often do: two in three organisations that made layoffs filled at least a quarter of the roles again, most of them within six months.
  4. It usually does not save money: once the roles were filled again, 73% of the organisations had saved nothing or lost money. A job filled again within a few months costs more than it saves, before counting the service, the overtime and the knowledge that were lost.
  5. The jobs come back changed: with other titles, at lower pay, through agencies or in other countries, which is what both Gartner and Forrester expect.

The data are thin: one count of announcements, one count of people hired back, and surveys run by firms with an interest in the answer. But they point the same way: replacing people with AI before the AI can do the whole job tends to cost a company twice, once to let people go and once to get the work done again.

Sources

  • US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS), via FRED: JTSHIR (hires rate), JTSLDR (layoffs and discharges rate), JTSLDL (layoffs and discharges, level).
  • Challenger, Gray & Christmas, job cuts reports: December 2023, December 2024, 2025 year-end, May 2026, June 2026, August 2026, October 2026; the AI cuts from the start of 2026 to the end of January, February, March, April, July and September as reported by HRD America, which match Challenger’s own figures for the other months.
  • Visier, The true cost of layoff boomerangs (February 2026) and The Layoff Boomerang Report (November 2025).
  • Careerminds, AI-led layoffs: what HR leaders wish they knew before making job cuts (February 2026). The headings of the page give some rounded or combined figures (75% cost more than they saved, 52.1% within six months) that do not match its own charts; this page uses the figures of the charts.
  • Orgvue, as reported by HR Dive and TechRadar (April 2025).
  • Gartner, as reported by TechRepublic (March 2026) and CX Today (June 2025).
  • Forrester, Predictions 2026: The Workforce Muddles Through Ambient Disruption (November 2025).
  • Klarna: CX Today, February 2024, CX Today, May 2025, TechCrunch, June 2025.
  • Commonwealth Bank of Australia: The Register, Bloomberg (August 2025).
  • Ford: TechCrunch (June 2026).

This post first appeared on Illustrations in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Latent Profile Analysis: Are There Personality Types?
item.description: Latent profile analysis of Big Five scores in R with mclust: model choice, BIC and ICL, entropy, stability, null models, and whether personality types exist.
item.content:encoded:
Latent profile analysis of Big Five scores in R with mclust: model choice, BIC and ICL, entropy, stability, null models, and whether personality types exist.

The question: types or dimensions?

The Big Five describe personality with five dimensions: everybody has a score on extraversion, neuroticism, agreeableness, conscientiousness and openness, and the scores vary smoothly from low to high. A second tradition looks for types: groups of people who share a whole pattern of traits.

  • Robins et al. (1996) and Asendorpf et al. (2001) described three replicable types: resilient (calm, sociable, agreeable, conscientious, open), overcontrolled (anxious and introverted) and undercontrolled (low agreeableness and low conscientiousness).
  • Gerlach et al. (2018), with more than a million online respondents, reported four types: average, reserved, self-centred and role model.

The dimensional approach is variable-centred: it asks how traits relate to each other and to outcomes. The typological approach is person-centred: it asks which kinds of people there are. Latent profile analysis (LPA) is the usual tool of the second. It assumes the population is a mixture of a few hidden subgroups, each with its own average trait profile, and estimates how many there are, what they look like and who belongs where.

This tutorial runs an LPA on the Big Five scores of almost 20,000 people, and shows step by step how easy it is to find profiles, and how hard it is to show that they are real.

Code 
library(mclust)     # Gaussian mixture models: latent profile analysis
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots side by side

1. The data and the five trait scores

The data are the online answers to the 50 items of the IPIP Big Five markers, described and validated on the IPIP-50 / OCEAN Validation and OCEAN pages. Each item is answered from 1 (disagree) to 5 (agree), with 0 for a missed item. We drop people with missed items, reverse the negatively keyed items (\(6 - x\), so 1 becomes 5), and average the ten items of each trait:

Code 
load("data/df_ocean.rda")
items <- c(paste0("E", 1:10), paste0("N", 1:10), paste0("A", 1:10), paste0("C", 1:10), paste0("O", 1:10))
reverse_items <- c("E2", "E4", "E6", "E8", "E10", "N2", "N4", "A1", "A3", "A5", "A7",
                   "C2", "C4", "C6", "C8", "O2", "O4", "O6")
d <- df_ocean[rowSums(df_ocean[, items] == 0) == 0, ]       # complete answers only
for (v in reverse_items) d[[v]] <- 6 - d[[v]]                # reverse keying: 1 <-> 5, 2 <-> 4
traits <- c(E = "Extraversion", N = "Neuroticism", A = "Agreeableness", C = "Conscientiousness", O = "Openness")
scores <- sapply(names(traits), function(t) rowMeans(d[, paste0(t, 1:10)]))   # mean of the 10 items, 1 to 5
z <- scale(scores)                                                            # standardised: mean 0, SD 1
c(people = nrow(z), dropped = nrow(df_ocean) - nrow(z))
 people dropped 
  19718       1

The traits are standardised, so a profile mean of +0.5 means half a standard deviation above the average respondent. Two features of the scores matter later: the traits are correlated, and some are skewed. The correlation plot is drawn with plot_corrplot() of the rwf package, and the skewness with its compute_skewness():

Code 
r <- cor(scores)
dimnames(r) <- list(traits, traits)
plot_corrplot(r, title = "Correlations of the five trait scores", base_size = 12)
Code 
round(sapply(as.data.frame(scores), compute_skewness), 2)
    E     N     A     C     O 
-0.04 -0.08 -0.76 -0.09 -0.47

Extraversion goes with agreeableness (r = 0.33) and against neuroticism (r = -0.26). Agreeableness (-0.76) and openness (-0.47) are skewed to the left: most people describe themselves as agreeable and open, and a long tail does not.

2. What latent profile analysis is

A mixture of normal distributions

LPA assumes that each person belongs to one of \(K\) hidden profiles. Within profile \(k\), the five scores \(\mathbf{x}\) follow a multivariate normal distribution with mean vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\) (the profile’s average pattern) and covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k\) (how much people within the profile differ, and how their traits go together). In the population, the scores then follow a mixture:

\[f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k \, \phi(\mathbf{x};\, \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)\]

  • \(\pi_k\) is the share of the population in profile \(k\) (the class proportions, summing to 1);
  • \(\phi\) is the density of the multivariate normal distribution.

Nobody’s profile is observed. The model gives each person a posterior probability of belonging to each profile, from Bayes’ rule:

\[\tau_{ik} = P(\text{person } i \text{ in profile } k \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = \frac{\pi_k \, \phi(\mathbf{x}_i;\, \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} \pi_j \, \phi(\mathbf{x}_i;\, \boldsymbol{\mu}_j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)}\]

The EM algorithm estimates everything by alternating two steps: compute the \(\tau_{ik}\) from the current parameters (E step), then re-estimate \(\pi_k\), \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\) and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k\) as averages weighted by the \(\tau_{ik}\) (M step), until nothing changes. EM finds a local maximum of the likelihood, so different starting points can end in different solutions (section 6).

Which covariance matrices?

The covariance matrices \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k\) are where the models differ. mclust names them with three letters (volume, shape, orientation; E = equal across profiles, V = varying, I = aligned with the axes). The four that matter for LPA:

mclust Covariances within a profile Same in every profile? Free parameters for 5 traits and \(K\) profiles
EEI Variances only, traits uncorrelated within a profile Yes \(5K + 5 + (K - 1)\)
VVI Variances only, traits uncorrelated within a profile No \(10K + (K - 1)\)
EEE Full covariance matrix: traits may correlate Yes \(5K + 15 + (K - 1)\)
VVV Full covariance matrix No \(20K + (K - 1)\)

The classic LPA, the default of most software, is EEI: the traits are assumed to be locally independent, uncorrelated within each profile, so every correlation between traits in the whole sample must come from differences between the profiles. Section 4 shows why this assumption is dangerous for personality data.

LPA and k-means

k-means also splits people into groups, but it is a limiting case of the simplest mixture: equal, spherical clusters, and every person assigned with certainty to the nearest centre. It has no probabilities, no likelihood and no fit indices, so it cannot say how many groups there are or how sure an assignment is. LPA can, at least in principle.

3. A first try: fit everything and let BIC choose

We fit the four models with 1 to 8 profiles. mclust starts EM from a hierarchical clustering of a random subset of 2,000 people (with more than 2,000 people), so we set a seed to make the result reproducible:

Code 
models <- c("EEI", "VVI", "EEE", "VVV")
set.seed(2026)
bic <- mclustBIC(z, G = 1:8, modelNames = models)
bic

2 -275035.0 -273158.9 -271502.6 -270787.9
