k-means, with its round, equal clusters, cuts the data in yet another way (ARI with the LPA solution 0.09): conventional, reserved (29%); open, reserved, disagreeable, anxious, disorganised (31%); outgoing, calm, warm, organised, open (40%). One cluster looks like the resilient type, and another combines the anxiety and introversion of the overcontrolled type with the low agreeableness and conscientiousness of the undercontrolled type. That may look like the classic typology, but k-means always returns exactly the number of clusters it is asked for, with roughly equal sizes, whether or not the data contain groups: three slices of one round cloud would look much the same.

8. Profiles, age and gender, carefully

Once the profiles exist, studies usually compare them on other variables. The simplest way assigns every person to their most likely profile (modal assignment) and compares the groups. With unclear classification this attenuates the differences, because many people are counted in the wrong profile. Weighting every person by their posterior probabilities instead keeps the uncertainty visible, but it attenuates the differences too (Bolck et al., 2004). Only three-step methods that correct for the classification error (Vermunt, 2010; Bakk et al., 2013) remove the bias; they are available in dedicated latent class software, not in mclust.

Code 
ok <- d$age >= 13 & d$age <= 80 & d$gender %in% 1:2         # plausible ages; 1 = male, 2 = female
female <- d$gender[ok] == 2
age <- d$age[ok]
tau_ok <- tau[ok, ]
round(rbind(
  women_modal    = tapply(female, assigned[ok], mean),
  women_weighted = colSums(tau_ok * female) / colSums(tau_ok),
  age_modal      = tapply(age, assigned[ok], mean),
  age_weighted   = colSums(tau_ok * age) / colSums(tau_ok)), 2)
                   1     2     3
women_modal     0.52  0.62  0.72
women_weighted  0.55  0.62  0.71
age_modal      24.19 26.22 29.65
age_weighted   24.62 26.30 29.37

With either method the profiles differ in their share of women (from 52% to 72% with modal assignment) and in mean age, and the weighted differences are, if anything, slightly smaller, as the attenuation argument predicts. The differences between the latent profiles themselves are probably larger than both estimates. But there is a simpler question behind the comparison: are the traits related to age and gender? The variable-centred answer needs no profiles at all:

Code 
round(rbind(r_with_age = cor(z[ok, ], age)[, 1], r_with_female = cor(z[ok, ], female)[, 1]), 2)
                 E     N    A    C     O
r_with_age    0.10 -0.16 0.16 0.21  0.08
r_with_female 0.05  0.17 0.21 0.03 -0.10

These correlations use all the information in the scores, with no classification error to correct.

9. Types or dimensions?

Put together, the evidence from these data:

Check Result Expected if there were types
BIC Rises to 8 profiles for every model Peaks at a small number
BIC in typeless data with the same skew and correlations Also rises to 8 Stays at 1
Diagonal models in one normal cloud 8 “profiles” 1
ICL 1 profile The number of types
Relative entropy, 3 profiles 0.52 Above .80
Random starts Best solution found by 1 of 10 Found by most starts
Split halves (ARI) 0.31 Close to 1

The profiles that LPA finds here are ways of cutting a continuous, skewed and correlated cloud of people into regions, not groups that exist apart from the method. This matches the debate around the four types of Gerlach et al. (2018), which other researchers could not reproduce robustly (Freudenstein et al., 2019).

That does not make LPA useless. It is the right tool when there is reason to expect qualitatively different groups, and the checks above are how to find out whether they are there. Profiles can also be a convenient description (“about a quarter of the sample combines high extraversion with high agreeableness”), as long as the report says that they summarise a continuum. For predicting outcomes, the five continuous scores keep more information than any profile membership.

10. Reporting the results in APA style

A report of an LPA (APA 7th edition) should say which models were compared and how the number of profiles was chosen, and give a fit table, the entropy, the class sizes and the profile means. With these data, an honest report states that no number of profiles was clearly supported. The numbers come from the R objects:

Code 
nz  <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
fmt <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",")

Method (data analysis):

Latent profile analyses of the five standardised trait scores (N = 19,718) were run with Gaussian mixture models in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the mclust package (Version 6.1.4; Scrucca et al., 2016). We compared models with uncorrelated traits within profiles (equal or varying variances) and with correlated traits (equal or varying covariance matrices), each with one to eight profiles, using the BIC, the ICL and the relative entropy. Because the traits were correlated and skewed, we compared the results with simulated data that had the same correlations and the same distribution of every trait but no subgroups. The three-profile solution was the best of 10 random starts, and its stability was examined in two random halves of the sample.

Results:

The BIC increased with every additional profile for all models, up to the maximum of eight, and it did so also in the simulated data without subgroups. The ICL favoured a single profile, ICL = 273,630, against 279,446 for two profiles (lower is better). A three-profile model with correlated traits classified people poorly (relative entropy = .52; 34% of respondents had no profile probability of at least .70), different random starts converged on different solutions, and the profiles did not replicate across random halves of the sample (adjusted Rand index = .31). We therefore found no support for distinct personality types in these data (Table 1).

Table 1

Fit of Latent Profile Models With Correlated Traits and Varying Covariance Matrices

Profiles Log-likelihood p BIC ICL Entropy Smallest profile
1 -136,716 20 273,630 273,630 100.0%
2 -135,191 41 270,788 279,446 .43 46.9%
3 -134,700 62 270,013 282,669 .47 18.3%
4 -134,242 83 269,306 284,103 .51 13.7%
5 -134,244 104 269,517 287,112 .49 13.5%
6 -134,037 125 269,310 288,652 .49 11.6%
7 -133,829 146 269,103 289,306 .52 7.2%
8 -133,643 167 268,937 290,373 .52 5.2%

Note. N = 19,718. p = number of free parameters. BIC and ICL are given in the usual convention, where lower is better (mclust reports them with the opposite sign). Entropy is the relative entropy of the posterior probabilities. All rows come from the same starting values; the three-profile solution described in the text is the best of 10 random starts.

Points to remember:

  • Report every model compared (covariance structures and numbers of profiles), not only the chosen one.
  • Give the BIC and a measure of classification quality (entropy, ICL, average posterior probabilities), and the size of the smallest profile.
  • Say how many random starts were used, and whether the best solution was found more than once.
  • Check the solution against a typeless null model and in a second sample or half before calling profiles “types”.
  • Cite R and the packages; citation() and citation("mclust") in R give the exact references.

11. Summary

What LPA does Models the population as a mixture of \(K\) normal distributions (profiles), each with its own mean and covariance matrix; gives every person a probability of belonging to each profile
Covariance models EEI/VVI: traits uncorrelated within profiles (classic LPA); EEE/VVV: correlated. Diagonal models invent profiles when traits are correlated
Choosing \(K\) BIC (in mclust, higher is better), ICL, relative entropy, smallest class size, interpretability, and theory; with large samples BIC alone keeps adding profiles
Classification quality Relative entropy and average posterior probabilities; above .80 for confident assignment
Local maxima Run EM from many random starts and keep the best log-likelihood; check that it is found repeatedly
Before calling them types Compare with a typeless null model (same correlations and skew), replicate in another sample, and check that the classification is clear
Covariates Modal assignment attenuates differences; weight by posterior probabilities, or use three-step methods
R mclustBIC(x, G = 1:8, modelNames = c("EEI", "VVI", "EEE", "VVV")), Mclust(), icl(), adjustedRandIndex(), predict()
Here No support for personality types in 19,718 sets of Big Five scores: the profiles behave like cuts through a continuum

References

Asendorpf, J. B., Borkenau, P., Ostendorf, F., & van Aken, M. A. G. (2001). Carving personality description at its joints: Confirmation of three replicable personality prototypes for both children and adults. European Journal of Personality, 15(3), 169–198.

Bakk, Z., Tekle, F. B., & Vermunt, J. K. (2013). Estimating the association between latent class membership and external variables using bias-adjusted three-step approaches. Sociological Methodology, 43(1), 272–311.

Bauer, D. J., & Curran, P. J. (2003). Distributional assumptions of growth mixture models: Implications for overextraction of latent trajectory classes. Psychological Methods, 8(3), 338–363.

Biernacki, C., Celeux, G., & Govaert, G. (2000). Assessing a mixture model for clustering with the integrated completed likelihood. IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, 22(7), 719–725.

Bolck, A., Croon, M., & Hagenaars, J. (2004). Estimating latent structure models with categorical variables: One-step versus three-step estimators. Political Analysis, 12(1), 3–27.

Freudenstein, J.-P., Strauch, C., Mussel, P., & Ziegler, M. (2019). Four personality types may be neither robust nor exhaustive. Nature Human Behaviour, 3(10), 1045–1046.

Gerlach, M., Farb, B., Revelle, W., & Nunes Amaral, L. A. (2018). A robust data-driven approach identifies four personality types across four large data sets. Nature Human Behaviour, 2(10), 735–742.

Goldberg, L. R. (1992). The development of markers for the Big-Five factor structure. Psychological Assessment, 4(1), 26–42.

Hubert, L., & Arabie, P. (1985). Comparing partitions. Journal of Classification, 2(1), 193–218.

Robins, R. W., John, O. P., Caspi, A., Moffitt, T. E., & Stouthamer-Loeber, M. (1996). Resilient, overcontrolled, and undercontrolled boys: Three replicable personality types. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 70(1), 157–171.

Scrucca, L., Fop, M., Murphy, T. B., & Raftery, A. E. (2016). mclust 5: Clustering, classification and density estimation using Gaussian finite mixture models. The R Journal, 8(1), 289–317.

Spurk, D., Hirschi, A., Wang, M., Valero, D., & Kauffeld, S. (2020). Latent profile analysis: A review and “how to” guide of its application within vocational behavior research. Journal of Vocational Behavior, 120, 103445.

Vermunt, J. K. (2010). Latent class modeling with covariates: Two improved three-step approaches. Political Analysis, 18(4), 450–469.

See also

  • rwf: the R package behind compute_skewness() and plot_corrplot() on this page

This post first appeared on Scale Validation in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Careless Responding: Screening Questionnaire Data in R
item.description: Finding careless responders in R on real DASS data: bogus items, response times, long-string, Mahalanobis, consistency indices, tested on known cases.
item.content:encoded:
Finding careless responders in R on real DASS data: bogus items, response times, long-string, Mahalanobis, consistency indices, tested on known cases.

The problem: answers that were not read

Online questionnaires are cheap, and so are their answers. Some people click through without reading: to reach the end, to get the feedback, or because they lost interest halfway. Studies that planted checks in their surveys found such careless (or insufficient-effort) responding in roughly 10% of respondents, often more in anonymous online samples (Meade & Craig, 2012; Curran, 2016).

A few careless answers can change results more than their number suggests:

  • Random answers add noise, which weakens correlations. On a scale where most people score low, such as a clinical symptom scale, random answers also look like symptoms: a random clicker scores near the middle of the scale, far above the typical healthy respondent.
  • The same answer to every item (straight-lining) does the opposite: it makes items look perfectly consistent, so it inflates reliability and correlations between scales.
  • Careless responders can create extra factors, for example a “factor” of the reverse-worded items that is really a factor of people who did not notice the wording (see the Rosenberg Self-Esteem page).

Careless answers come in a few typical patterns:

Pattern What it looks like Typical sign
Random Answers chosen by chance Inconsistent with other answers, unusual profile, often fast
Straight-lining The same answer again and again Long runs of one answer, almost no variability
Patterned A zigzag such as 1-2-3-4-3-2 or 1-4-1-4 Regular, but unrelated to the content
Partial Careful at first, careless later (fatigue) Signs only in the second half

There are two ways to find them. Direct checks are built into the questionnaire in advance: items with an obvious right answer, instructed items (“choose agree here”) or questions about one’s own effort. Post hoc indices are computed from the answers and response times afterwards. This guide computes all the common ones by hand on real data, tests them on careless responders whose identity we know, and shows how to combine them and how to report the screening.

Code 
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots together
library(pROC)       # ROC curves and the AUC

1. The data

The data are the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (DASS-42) answered online in 2017-2019 at the Open-Source Psychometrics Project, the same data as the DASS-42 validation page. That page uses the cleaned data; here we start before any cleaning, because finding the careless records is the point. data/prepare_careless.R keeps every record that answered all 42 items.

The survey had three features that make it ideal for this guide:

  • Each item was shown on its own screen, in a random order for each person, and the time to answer it was recorded.
  • After the DASS came a vocabulary checklist of 16 words (“tick the words whose meaning you are sure you know”). Three of them, cuivocal, florted and verdid, do not exist.
  • The Ten Item Personality Inventory (TIPI) has five pairs of opposite items, such as “extraverted, enthusiastic” and “reserved, quiet”.
Code 
load("data/df_careless.rda")
d <- df_careless
items <- paste0("Q", 1:42)
X <- as.matrix(d[, items])                       # answers 1-4, in item order
O <- as.matrix(d[, paste0("O", 1:42)])           # O1 = the item shown first, O2 = second, ...
n <- nrow(X)
key <- list(Depression = c(3, 5, 10, 13, 16, 17, 21, 24, 26, 31, 34, 37, 38, 42),
            Anxiety    = c(2, 4, 7, 9, 15, 19, 20, 23, 25, 28, 30, 36, 40, 41),
            Stress     = c(1, 6, 8, 11, 12, 14, 18, 22, 27, 29, 32, 33, 35, 39))
scores <- sapply(key, function(k) rowSums(X[, k] - 1))   # DASS scoring: answers 1-4 count as 0-3
c(records = n, items = ncol(X))
records   items 
  39775      42

The answers are 1 (did not apply to me at all) to 4 (applied to me very much). Each scale has 14 items and a score from 0 to 42.

Two helpers, used throughout. The first puts each person’s answers back in the order they saw them; the second computes a correlation within each person (each row) at once:

Code 
# answers in the order each person saw the items: column k = the answer to the k-th item shown
in_shown_order <- function(X, O) sapply(seq_len(ncol(X)), function(k) X[cbind(seq_len(nrow(X)), O[, k])])
# correlation of row i of A with row i of B, for every row
rowcor <- function(A, B) {
  A <- A - rowMeans(A); B <- B - rowMeans(B)
  rowSums(A * B) / sqrt(rowSums(A^2) * rowSums(B^2))
}
S <- in_shown_order(X, O)

2. Bogus items: words that do not exist

A bogus (or infrequency) item has only one honest answer. Claiming to know a word that does not exist is a sign that the person did not read, or that they claim more than they know.

Code 
table(fake_words_claimed = d$fake_words)
fake_words_claimed
    0     1     2     3 
34583  4044   822   326
Code 
round(100 * mean(d$fake_words >= 1), 1)   # % who claimed at least one
[1] 13.1

13.1% claimed at least one non-existent word, far more than any estimate of careless responding. Do they answer the DASS carelessly? We will meet the indices below; as a preview, compare two of them, and the number of real words claimed:

Code 
preview <- data.frame(
  real_words   = d$real_words,
  longest_run  = apply(S, 1, function(v) max(rle(v)$lengths)),          # longest run of one answer
  person_total = rowcor(X, matrix(colMeans(X), n, 42, byrow = TRUE)))   # agreement with the typical profile
profile_of <- function(group)
  t(sapply(split(preview, group), function(s) c(people = nrow(s), colMeans(s, na.rm = TRUE))))
round(profile_of(pmin(d$fake_words, 2)), 2)   # 0, 1, and 2 or 3 fake words
  people real_words longest_run person_total
0  34583       6.64        6.81         0.32
1   4044       8.65        7.21         0.29
2   1148       9.66        8.25         0.26

People who claim one fake word answer the DASS much like everyone else: their longest run of identical answers and their person-total correlation (section 7) are close to those of people who claimed none. What they do differently is claim more real words too: they overclaim. One fake word can be an honest mistake (florted looks like a real word); two or three are much less likely. As the rule for this guide we take two or more fake words, which flags 1148 people (2.9%). The DASS-42 validation page used the stricter “any fake word”; both are defensible if decided in advance.

Bogus items work best when the right answer is obvious to anyone reading (“I have never used a computer” in an online survey) and are spread through the questionnaire, so that they catch carelessness where it happens.

3. Response time

Reading a sentence and choosing an answer takes time. The most common rule, from Huang et al. (2012), flags anyone faster than 2 seconds per item. Here every item had its own screen, so we have the time for each item; we use each person’s median item time, which a single long pause cannot distort.

Code 
ggplot(d, aes(median_rt)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 80, fill = "#0082c8", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(1, 2), linetype = "dashed", colour = c("#E74C3C", "#f39c12")) +
  annotate("text", x = c(1, 2), y = Inf, label = c("1 s", "2 s"), vjust = 1.5, hjust = -0.2, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20)) +
  labs(title = "Median time per item (log scale)", x = "seconds", y = "people")
Code 
speed <- cut(d$median_rt, c(0, 1, 2, 3, Inf), labels = c("under 1 s", "1-2 s", "2-3 s", "over 3 s"))
speed_profile <- profile_of(speed)
round(speed_profile, 2)
          people real_words longest_run person_total
under 1 s    262       5.56       25.26         0.04
1-2 s       1501       8.07       14.58         0.29
2-3 s       9960       7.65        7.92         0.32
over 3 s   28052       6.62        5.95         0.32

People with a median under 1 second per item are clearly careless: they claim fewer real words than anyone else, their longest run of one answer averages about 25 items, and their answers barely follow the typical profile (person-total near 0). Nobody reads a sentence in under a second. People at 1-2 seconds are a mixture: their person-total correlation is normal (0.29), but their longest runs (14.6 on average) are about twice those of slower people, a sign that some of them are straight-lining. Huang et al.’s 2-second rule came from surveys with many items per page; with one short item per screen and one click per answer, fast but genuine readers can answer in under 2 seconds. Here the 2-second rule would flag 1727 people (4.3%). We use 1 second, which flags 261 (0.7%), and leave the straight-liners among the 1-2 second group to the long-string rule of section 4. The lesson is general: a time cut-off depends on the format of the survey, and should be checked against other indices.

4. Long-string: the same answer again and again

The long-string index is the longest run of identical consecutive answers (Johnson, 2005). It must be computed in the order the person saw the items: here every person had a different order, so a run in item number order means nothing.

Code 
longest_run <- function(S) {          # S: answers in the order shown, one row per person
  run <- best <- rep(1, nrow(S)); answer <- S[, 1]
  for (k in 2:ncol(S)) {
    run <- ifelse(S[, k] == S[, k - 1], run + 1, 1)
    longer <- run > best
    answer[longer] <- S[longer, k]      # the answer that is repeated in the longest run
    best <- pmax(best, run)
  }
  data.frame(longstring = best, repeated = answer)
}
ls <- longest_run(S)
quantile(ls$longstring, c(.5, .9, .95, .99))
 50%  90%  95%  99% 
 5.0 12.0 17.3 37.0

Half the people never give the same answer more than 5 times in a row. Runs of 21 or more, half the questionnaire, are rare:

Code 
ls$repeated_answer <- factor(ls$repeated, 1:4, c("1 did not apply", "2", "3", "4 applied very much"))
ggplot(subset(ls, longstring >= 10), aes(longstring, fill = repeated_answer)) +
  geom_bar() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 20.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#95A5A6", "#f39c12", "#E74C3C", "#8E44AD")) +
  labs(title = "Long runs of one answer (runs of 10 or more), by the answer repeated",
       x = "longest run of identical answers", y = "people", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
Code 
table(answer_repeated_42_times = ls$repeated[ls$longstring == 42])
answer_repeated_42_times
  1   2   3   4 
110  10   6 123

The bar at 42 is people who gave the same answer to every item. Which answer matters. Did not apply to me at all, 42 times, is what a person without symptoms would honestly say. Applied to me very much, 42 times, would mean the worst level of every symptom, including dry mouth, trembling and difficulty swallowing, all at once: possible, but far less likely than a person holding down one key. Our rule therefore flags runs of 21 or more, unless the repeated answer is did not apply:

Code 
long_flag <- ls$longstring >= 21 & ls$repeated != 1
c(flagged = sum(long_flag), percent = round(100 * mean(long_flag), 1),
  median_seconds_flagged = median(d$median_rt[long_flag]), median_seconds_others = median(d$median_rt[!long_flag]))
               flagged                percent median_seconds_flagged  median_seconds_others 
               770.000                  1.900                  2.055                  3.610

The flagged people also answered faster than the rest (median 2.05 s per item against 3.61 s), which supports the rule. Half the questionnaire is still a judgement: a person with severe symptoms could honestly give applied to me very much many times in a row, so the cut-off should be generous and decided in advance. On a scale with reverse-worded items there is no exception for any answer: the same answer to items that mean opposite things is a contradiction.

5. Intra-individual response variability (IRV)

The IRV is the standard deviation of a person’s answers across the items (Dunn et al., 2018):

\[\text{IRV}_i = \sqrt{\frac{1}{k - 1} \sum_{j=1}^{k} (x_{ij} - \bar x_i)^2}\]

A very low IRV means the same few answers throughout, like straight-lining. A very high IRV means answers jumping between the extremes, as random or zigzag clicking does. IRV is a measure of spread, not of content, so it cannot tell a genuinely mixed profile from noise; it is most useful next to the other indices.

6. Mahalanobis distance

The Mahalanobis distance measures how far a person’s whole answer profile lies from the average profile, taking the correlations between the items into account:

\[D^2_i = (\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}})^\top \, \mathbf{S}^{-1} \, (\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}})\]

where \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}\) is the vector of item means and \(\mathbf{S}\) the covariance matrix of the items. A profile is far away when it combines answers that rarely go together: severe on one depression item but none on its close neighbours, for example. If the answers were multivariate normal, \(D^2\) would follow a \(\chi^2\) distribution with \(k\) = 42 degrees of freedom, and the usual cut-off is its 99.9th percentile:

Code 
irv <- apply(X, 1, sd)
md  <- mahalanobis(X, colMeans(X), cov(X))
md_cut <- qchisq(0.999, df = 42)
c(cut_off = md_cut, expected_share = 0.001, observed_share = mean(md > md_cut))
       cut_off expected_share observed_share 
   76.08376271     0.00100000     0.06328096
Code 
p_irv <- ggplot(data.frame(irv), aes(irv)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "#0082c8", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  labs(title = "IRV: SD of each person's answers", x = "IRV", y = "people")
grid_md <- data.frame(x = seq(0, 180, length.out = 400))
grid_md$y <- dchisq(grid_md$x, 42) * n * 3        # chi-square density scaled to the histogram (bin width 3)
p_md <- ggplot(data.frame(md), aes(md)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 3, fill = "#0082c8", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_line(data = grid_md, aes(x, y), colour = "#E74C3C", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = md_cut, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Mahalanobis D² and χ²(42)", x = "D²", y = "people")
p_irv + p_md

The \(\chi^2\) cut-off should flag 0.1% of people; it flags 6.3%. The histogram shows why: the distances have a much longer right tail than the red \(\chi^2\) curve. The answers are four-point ratings, most of them piled at did not apply, nowhere near multivariate normal, so the \(\chi^2\) distribution is the wrong yardstick. Section 11 shows who these “outliers” are: mostly not careless people at all.

7. Consistency indices

An attentive person answers similar items similarly. Three indices turn that into a number per person, each a correlation computed within the person.

Even-odd consistency

Split every scale into its odd- and even-numbered items, score each half, and correlate the odd-half scores with the even-half scores across the scales, within each person; then correct the correlation to full length with the Spearman-Brown formula, \(r_{SB} = 2r / (1 + r)\) (Johnson, 2005). An attentive person’s two halves agree; a random responder’s do not.

Code 
half <- function(k, start) paste0("Q", k[seq(start, length(k), by = 2)])
odd  <- sapply(key, function(k) rowMeans(X[, half(k, 1)]))
even <- sapply(key, function(k) rowMeans(X[, half(k, 2)]))
r_eo <- pmax(rowcor(odd, even), -0.999)            # keep r away from -1, where 2r / (1 + r) explodes
even_odd <- pmax(2 * r_eo / (1 + r_eo), -1)        # Spearman-Brown; values below -1 are capped at -1
summary(even_odd)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
-1.0000  0.4932  0.9023  0.5492  0.9841  1.0000    1463

The index works well for questionnaires with many short subscales: the HEXACO page uses 24 facets and the IPIP-NEO-120 page 30. The DASS has only three scales, so each person’s correlation rests on three pairs of numbers: it is often exactly 1 or −1 by chance, and it is undefined (NA) for the 1463 people whose half-scores do not vary. Section 8 shows what that costs.

Psychometric synonyms

Instead of halves of scales, use pairs of items that are highly correlated in the whole sample (Meade & Craig, 2012), here every pair with \(r > .60\), and correlate each person’s answers to the first item of each pair with their answers to the second:

Code 
R <- cor(X)
pairs <- which(R > .60 & upper.tri(R), arr.ind = TRUE)    # synonym pairs
nrow(pairs)
[1] 55
Code 
synonyms <- rowcor(X[, pairs[, 1]], X[, pairs[, 2]])
summary(synonyms)
     Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max.       NAs 
-0.713624  0.007431  0.127464  0.167766  0.279145  1.000000      1251

The 55 pairs give a more stable index than three half-scales. Psychometric antonyms do the same with strongly negatively correlated pairs; the DASS has no reverse-worded items, so it has none. The TIPI has five pairs of opposites, which allow a simpler check, the “agree with both” count used on the Rosenberg Self-Esteem page: agreeing strongly (6 or 7 on the 7-point scale) with both “extraverted, enthusiastic” and “reserved, quiet” is a contradiction.

Code 
tipi <- as.matrix(d[, paste0("TIPI", 1:10)])
agree_both <- rowSums(tipi[, 1:5] >= 6 & tipi[, 6:10] >= 6, na.rm = TRUE)   # pairs 1-6, 2-7, 3-8, 4-9, 5-10
table(opposite_pairs_agreed = agree_both)
opposite_pairs_agreed
    0     1     2     3     4     5 
28353  8827  2070   416    65    44

525 people agreed strongly with both opposites in three or more of the five pairs. Five pairs are too few for a reliable index, and the TIPI came after the DASS, so this check describes attention later in the survey; we report it but do not use it as a rule.

Person-total correlation

The person-total correlation asks whether a person’s profile has the usual shape: high on the items most people endorse, low on those few people endorse. It is the correlation between the person’s 42 answers and the 42 item means of the sample (Curran, 2016):

Code 
item_means <- colMeans(X)
person_total <- rowcor(X, matrix(item_means, n, 42, byrow = TRUE))
summary(person_total)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
-0.6472  0.1811  0.3359  0.3172  0.4723  0.8357     249

Attentive people correlate positively with the typical profile; a random responder’s correlation is near 0. The index is undefined for people who gave the same answer to all 42 items (no variability), and it is low for people who answer almost everything with did not apply, whose few other answers carry little information. That is a reason not to use it alone.

Code 
consistency <- rbind(data.frame(index = "even-odd (3 scales)", value = even_odd),
                     data.frame(index = "synonyms (r > .60 pairs)", value = synonyms),
                     data.frame(index = "person-total", value = person_total))
consistency$index <- factor(consistency$index, levels = unique(consistency$index))   # panels in the order of the text
ggplot(na.omit(consistency), aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#0082c8", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~index, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Three within-person consistency indices", x = "correlation", y = "people")

The even-odd index piles up at 1 and −1, the sign of a correlation computed from three points; the synonym and person-total indices are smooth.

8. Testing the indices on known careless responders

In real data we never know who was careless, so we cannot tell how well an index works. A simulation can: take people who look attentive, add careless responders whose answers we generate, and see which index finds them.

  • Attentive people: 2,000 records drawn at random from those who claimed no fake word and took at least 2 seconds per item. They are selected on the direct checks only, so that none of the pattern indices we are testing has a head start.
  • Careless people, 50 of each kind, each given the presentation order of a real person:
    • random: every answer drawn at random from 1-4;
    • straight-lining: one answer repeated, with 10% of the answers changed at random (nobody is perfectly consistent);
    • patterned: a zigzag (1-2-3-4-3-2-… or 1-4-1-4-…) in the order the items were shown;
    • half random: a real attentive person’s answers for the first 21 items shown, random answers for the last 21.

Response times and the vocabulary checklist cannot be tested this way: we would have to invent the careless people’s times and ticks, and the test would only find what we put in.

Code 
set.seed(42)
pool <- which(d$fake_words == 0 & d$median_rt >= 2)
attentive <- sample(pool, 2000)
k <- 50
random <- matrix(sample(1:4, k * 42, replace = TRUE), k)
straight <- t(sapply(1:k, function(i) {
  v <- rep(sample(1:4, 1), 42)
  changed <- runif(42) < 0.10
  v[changed] <- sample(1:4, sum(changed), replace = TRUE)
  v
}))
order_pat <- O[sample(pool, k), ]
patterned <- t(sapply(1:k, function(i) {
  cycle <- if (runif(1) < 0.5) c(1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2) else c(1, 4)
  start <- sample(length(cycle), 1)
  shown <- rep(cycle, 42)[start:(start + 41)]   # the zigzag, in the order the items were shown
  v <- integer(42); v[order_pat[i, ]] <- shown  # back to item order
  v
}))
source_half <- sample(setdiff(pool, attentive), k)
order_half <- O[source_half, ]
half_random <- X[source_half, ]
for (i in 1:k) half_random[i, order_half[i, 22:42]] <- sample(1:4, 21, replace = TRUE)
Xs <- rbind(X[attentive, ], random, straight, patterned, half_random)
Os <- rbind(O[attentive, ], O[sample(pool, k), ], O[sample(pool, k), ], order_pat, order_half)
type <- factor(rep(c("attentive", "random", "straight-lining", "patterned", "half random"), c(2000, k, k, k, k)),
               levels = c("attentive", "random", "straight-lining", "patterned", "half random"))

All the indices again, now on the mixed sample (the means, covariances and synonym pairs come from that sample, as they would in practice):

Code 
indices_of <- function(X, O) {
  S <- in_shown_order(X, O)
  odd  <- sapply(key, function(k) rowMeans(X[, half(k, 1)]))
  even <- sapply(key, function(k) rowMeans(X[, half(k, 2)]))
  r_eo <- pmax(rowcor(odd, even), -0.999)
  R <- cor(X); pr <- which(R > .60 & upper.tri(R), arr.ind = TRUE)
  run <- longest_run(S)
  data.frame(longstring = run$longstring, repeated = run$repeated,
             irv = apply(X, 1, sd),
             mahalanobis = mahalanobis(X, colMeans(X), cov(X)),
             even_odd = pmax(2 * r_eo / (1 + r_eo), -1),
             synonyms = rowcor(X[, pr[, 1]], X[, pr[, 2]]),
             person_total = rowcor(X, matrix(colMeans(X), nrow(X), 42, byrow = TRUE)))
}
sim <- indices_of(Xs, Os)

For each index and each kind of careless responder, the AUC is the chance that a randomly chosen careless responder looks more suspicious on that index than a randomly chosen attentive person: 0.5 is no better than chance, 1 is perfect. IRV appears twice, because both very low and very high values are suspicious. Undefined values (no variability in the answers) count as the most suspicious.

Code 
suspicious_if <- c(longstring = "high", irv = "low", irv = "high", mahalanobis = "high",
                   even_odd = "low", synonyms = "low", person_total = "low")
labels <- c("long-string", "IRV (low)", "IRV (high)", "Mahalanobis", "even-odd", "synonyms", "person-total")
auc_tab <- sapply(levels(type)[-1], function(t) {
  keep <- type %in% c("attentive", t)
  y <- as.integer(type[keep] == t)
  mapply(function(v, direction) {
    x <- sim[keep, v]
    if (direction == "low") x <- -x                        # higher = more suspicious
    x[is.na(x)] <- max(x, na.rm = TRUE) + 1                # no variability: most suspicious
    as.numeric(auc(roc(y, x, direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)))
  }, names(suspicious_if), suspicious_if)
})
rownames(auc_tab) <- labels
round(auc_tab, 2)
             random straight-lining patterned half random
long-string    0.16            0.96      0.00        0.37
IRV (low)      0.09            0.88      0.13        0.17
IRV (high)     0.91            0.12      0.87        0.83
Mahalanobis    0.99            0.25      0.97        0.96
even-odd       0.70            0.81      0.70        0.61
synonyms       0.72            0.91      0.69        0.68
person-total   0.90            0.91      0.88        0.82
Code 
auc_long <- data.frame(index = factor(rep(labels, ncol(auc_tab)), levels = rev(labels)),
                       pattern = factor(rep(colnames(auc_tab), each = nrow(auc_tab)), levels = colnames(auc_tab)),
                       auc = as.vector(auc_tab))
ggplot(auc_long, aes(pattern, index, fill = auc)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", auc)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#E74C3C", mid = "white", high = "#0082c8", midpoint = 0.5, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "AUC: how well each index separates careless from attentive people",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "AUC")

Each index catches some patterns and misses others:

  • Long-string finds straight-lining (AUC = 0.96) and nothing else. Its AUC for random and zigzag answers is far below 0.5: attentive people repeat answers more often than random clickers do, and a zigzag never repeats at all.
  • Mahalanobis finds random, zigzag and half-random answers (0.99, 0.97 and 0.96) but not straight-lining (0.25): a row of 2s or 3s sits close to the average profile.
  • IRV works in both directions: low values find straight-lining, high values the jumpy patterns.
  • Person-total is the best all-rounder, between 0.82 and 0.91 for every pattern.
  • Even-odd is the weakest here, as expected from three scales.

So screening needs several indices, chosen to cover the patterns: at least one for straight-lining (long-string or low IRV) and one for random-like answers (Mahalanobis, person-total or synonyms).

9. Putting them together: multiple hurdles

A common approach is a set of hurdles, each with its own rule, decided before looking at the results (Curran, 2016). For these data:

  1. Bogus words: claimed two or more of the three non-existent words.
  2. Too fast: median time per item under 1 second.
  3. Straight-lining: 21 or more identical answers in a row (in the order shown), unless the answer was did not apply.
  4. Random-like answers: an unusual profile and one that does not follow the typical shape: Mahalanobis \(D^2\) above the \(\chi^2\) cut-off and person-total \(r\) below .20.

The fourth rule combines two indices because each alone flags many attentive people (section 11): the Mahalanobis distance flags genuine extreme scorers, whose profiles still have the typical shape, and the person-total correlation flags people who answer almost everything with did not apply, whose profiles are not unusual. Requiring both keeps the random-like profiles and spares both groups. In the simulation:

Code 
rule_long   <- function(ind) ind$longstring >= 21 & ind$repeated != 1
rule_random <- function(ind, cut) ind$mahalanobis > cut & !is.na(ind$person_total) & ind$person_total < .20
caught <- data.frame(straight_lining_rule = rule_long(sim), random_like_rule = rule_random(sim, md_cut))
caught$either <- caught$straight_lining_rule | caught$random_like_rule
round(100 * sapply(caught, function(r) tapply(r, type, mean)))   # % of each kind flagged
                straight_lining_rule random_like_rule either
attentive                          1                1      3
random                             0               88     88
straight-lining                   28                0     28
patterned                          0               52     52
half random                        0               46     46

The two pattern rules together flag 2.9% of the attentive people and catch 88% of the random responders, 52% of the zigzags, 46% of the half-random and 28% of the straight-liners. The straight-liners escape for two reasons: those who repeated did not apply are spared by design, and the 10% of changed answers break many runs before they reach 21. Careless responding that is careless only some of the time is the hardest to find. In real data the time and bogus-word rules add to these, since they catch people the pattern rules miss.

Now on the real data:

Code 
rules <- data.frame(
  bogus_words     = d$fake_words >= 2,
  too_fast        = d$median_rt < 1,
  straight_lining = ls$longstring >= 21 & ls$repeated != 1,
  random_like     = md > md_cut & !is.na(person_total) & person_total < .20)
flagged <- Reduce(`|`, rules)
data.frame(flagged = colSums(rules), percent = round(100 * colMeans(rules), 1))
                flagged percent
bogus_words        1148     2.9
too_fast            261     0.7
straight_lining     770     1.9
random_like         936     2.4
Code 
c(flagged_by_any = sum(flagged), percent = round(100 * mean(flagged), 1))
flagged_by_any        percent 
        2849.0            7.2
Code 
table(number_of_rules_failed = rowSums(rules))
number_of_rules_failed
    0     1     2     3 
36926  2605   222    22

2849 people (7.2%) fail at least one hurdle, within the usual range for online samples. Most fail only one: the hurdles find different people, which is why there are several. The indices themselves are only loosely related (Spearman correlations):

Code 
all_indices <- data.frame(fake_words = d$fake_words, median_rt = d$median_rt, longstring = ls$longstring,
                          irv, mahalanobis = md, even_odd, synonyms, person_total)
round(cor(all_indices, method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs"), 2)
             fake_words median_rt longstring   irv mahalanobis even_odd synonyms person_total
fake_words         1.00     -0.11       0.01  0.00        0.00     0.02     0.03        -0.05
median_rt         -0.11      1.00      -0.21  0.12        0.18    -0.08    -0.12         0.00
longstring         0.01     -0.21       1.00 -0.54       -0.47    -0.08    -0.17        -0.19
irv                0.00      0.12      -0.54  1.00        0.88     0.17     0.29         0.28
mahalanobis        0.00      0.18      -0.47  0.88        1.00    -0.04    -0.01         0.00
even_odd           0.02     -0.08      -0.08  0.17       -0.04     1.00     0.37         0.25
synonyms           0.03     -0.12      -0.17  0.29       -0.01     0.37     1.00         0.21
person_total      -0.05      0.00      -0.19  0.28        0.00     0.25     0.21         1.00

Only IRV and the Mahalanobis distance are strongly related (0.88), and long-string goes with low IRV (-0.54). Claiming fake words is unrelated to every pattern index, and response time only weakly related (faster people have longer runs, -0.21). Careless responding is not one thing, and no single index measures all of it.

10. What screening changes

Compare the results with all records, with the people who passed every hurdle, and with the people flagged. Reliability uses compute_raw_alpha() of the rwf package (Cronbach’s alpha from the covariance matrix). The last column is the correlation of the depression score with TIPI emotional stability (“calm, emotionally stable” and, reversed, “anxious, easily upset”):

Code 
stability <- (8 - tipi[, 4] + tipi[, 9]) / 2
describe_group <- function(sel) {
  alpha <- sapply(key, function(k) compute_raw_alpha(as.data.frame(X[sel, k])))
  r <- cor(scores[sel, ])
  c(people = sum(sel), alpha_depression = alpha[[1]], alpha_anxiety = alpha[[2]], alpha_stress = alpha[[3]],
    r_depression_anxiety = r[1, 2], r_depression_stress = r[1, 3], r_anxiety_stress = r[2, 3],
    depression_mean = mean(scores[sel, 1]),
    r_depression_stability = cor(scores[sel, 1], stability[sel], use = "complete.obs"))
}
compare <- rbind(all = describe_group(rep(TRUE, n)), passed = describe_group(!flagged), flagged = describe_group(flagged),
                 `flagged: straight-lining` = describe_group(rules$straight_lining),
                 `flagged: random-like` = describe_group(rules$random_like))
round(compare, 3)
                         people alpha_depression alpha_anxiety alpha_stress r_depression_anxiety r_depression_stress r_anxiety_stress depression_mean r_depression_stability
all                       39775            0.956         0.916        0.928                0.670               0.740            0.802          21.060                 -0.526
passed                    36926            0.956         0.911        0.927                0.658               0.733            0.795          20.727                 -0.527
flagged                    2849            0.954         0.930        0.936                0.762               0.781            0.854          25.383                 -0.514
flagged: straight-lining    770            0.987         0.960        0.977                0.945               0.975            0.946          36.268                 -0.550
flagged: random-like        936            0.805         0.625        0.681                0.311               0.205            0.589          21.173                 -0.153

The two kinds of careless responding push the results in opposite directions:

  • The straight-liners look extremely consistent: their alphas range from 0.96 to 0.99 and their scales correlate 0.94 to 0.97, because the same answer everywhere makes every item agree with every other. They also score very high on depression (mean 36.3 of 42), since most of their runs are applied to me very much.
  • The random-like group shows the opposite, as noise would: lower alphas (0.62 to 0.80), weaker correlations between the scales (0.20 to 0.59), and a depression score that hardly relates to emotional stability (-0.15, against -0.53 in the people who passed).

Mixed into the whole sample, the two partly cancel out. Removing all the flagged people changes little here: the alphas stay within .01, and the depression-stress correlation goes from 0.74 to 0.73. Two lessons follow. A high alpha is not evidence that the data are clean: straight-lining raises it. And with only 7% flagged among almost 40,000 people the totals barely move, but in a sample of 200 a handful of straight-liners or random clickers can decide whether a correlation or a factor shows up at all.

11. Over-screening: the danger of Mahalanobis alone

Screening can also remove people who answered with care. The Mahalanobis distance with the \(\chi^2\) cut-off flagged 2517 people. Most of them passed every other hurdle:

Code 
md_only <- md > md_cut & !flagged
group <- ifelse(md_only, "Mahalanobis only", ifelse(flagged, "failed a hurdle", "passed"))
round(t(sapply(split(data.frame(median_rt = d$median_rt, person_total, depression = scores[, 1],
                                anxiety = scores[, 2]), group),
               function(s) c(people = nrow(s), apply(s, 2, median, na.rm = TRUE)))), 2)
                 people median_rt person_total depression anxiety
failed a hurdle    2849      2.99         0.15         25      24
Mahalanobis only   1540      3.98         0.35         25      17
passed            35386      3.61         0.35         20      14

The 1540 people flagged only by the Mahalanobis distance took longer per item than those who passed (median 3.98 s against 3.61 s), their profiles still follow the typical shape (person-total 0.35), and they report more symptoms. They look like careful people with unusual, often severe, symptom profiles: exactly the people a clinical scale exists to find. Removing them would have cut 3.9% of the sample and biased every result towards milder symptoms.

Code 
plot_df <- data.frame(group = factor(group, levels = c("passed", "Mahalanobis only", "failed a hurdle")),
                      median_rt = d$median_rt, depression = scores[, 1])
g1 <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(median_rt, colour = group)) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 1) + scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 2, 3, 5, 10)) +
  labs(title = "Time per item", x = "median seconds per item (log)", y = "density", colour = NULL)
g2 <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(depression, colour = group)) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 1, adjust = 1.5) +
  labs(title = "Depression score", x = "DASS depression (0-42)", y = "density", colour = NULL)
(g1 + g2 + plot_layout(guides = "collect")) & scale_colour_manual(values = c("#0082c8", "#f39c12", "#E74C3C")) &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Multivariate outlier rules come from settings where outliers are errors. In questionnaire data an unusual profile is often a real one. Use the Mahalanobis distance together with an index of careless patterns, or with an empirical cut-off, never alone.

12. Reporting the screening in APA style

Decide the screening rules before looking at the results, ideally in a preregistration, and report every rule with the number of people it excluded, so that readers can judge, and repeat, the screening. A sensitivity analysis with and without the exclusions shows whether the conclusions depend on them.

Code 
f1 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero

Method (data screening):

Before the analyses, we screened the 39,775 complete records for careless responding with four rules decided in advance: claiming to know two or more of three non-existent words in a vocabulary checklist; a median response time below 1 s per item; 21 or more identical consecutive answers in the order of presentation, other than did not apply to me at all; and a random-like answer pattern, defined as a Mahalanobis distance above the 99.9th percentile of the χ²(42) distribution together with a person-total correlation below .20 (Curran, 2016; Meade & Craig, 2012). The indices were computed in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

In total, 2,849 respondents (7.2%) failed at least one rule and were excluded (Table 1), leaving 36,926. Most excluded respondents (91.4%) failed a single rule. Internal consistency was high with and without the excluded respondents (depression α = .96 and .96), and excluding them reduced the correlation between the depression and stress scales from r = .74 to r = .73. A Mahalanobis distance rule alone would have excluded a further 1,540 respondents, who answered more slowly and reported more symptoms than the retained respondents; it was therefore used only in combination with the person-total correlation.

Table 1

Careless-Responding Screening Rules and Exclusions

Rule n flagged % n flagged by this rule only
Claimed two or more non-existent words 1148 2.9 1041
Median response time below 1 s per item 261 0.7 93
21 or more identical consecutive answers (other than did not apply) 770 1.9 609
Mahalanobis D² above χ²(42) 99.9th percentile and person-total r < .20 936 2.4 862
Any rule 2849 7.2

Note. N = 39,775 complete records. Respondents could fail more than one rule.

Points to remember:

  • Report each rule, its cut-off and its rationale, the number excluded by each and in total, and when the rules were decided.
  • Prefer rules that a reader can recompute; avoid vague criteria such as “suspicious patterns”.
  • Show whether the main results change without the exclusions.
  • Do not screen on the outcome itself (for example, removing the highest scorers because they look extreme).
  • Cite R and the packages; citation() in R gives the exact reference.

13. Summary

Index Catches Misses Watch out for
Bogus / infrequency items People who do not read Careful overclaimers look the same Plausible mistakes; use clear items, or require two
Response time Very fast clicking Slow careless people The cut-off depends on the survey format
Long-string Straight-lining Random and zigzag answers Compute in the order shown; a run of did not apply can be honest
IRV Low: straight-lining; high: random, zigzag Content: a mixed profile is not noise Use next to other indices
Mahalanobis Random, zigzag, partly random Straight-lining Over-flags genuine extreme profiles; χ² cut-off wrong for skewed ratings
Even-odd Random answers, given many subscales Everything, with three scales Needs many short subscales
Synonyms / antonyms Inconsistent answers Consistent careless patterns Needs enough highly correlated pairs
Person-total All patterns fairly well People who answer almost everything the same Low for genuine low scorers
Overall Several hurdles, chosen to cover the patterns, decided in advance and reported one by one High alpha is not a sign of clean data

References

Curran, P. G. (2016). Methods for the detection of carelessly invalid responses in survey data. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 66, 4–19.

Dunn, A. M., Heggestad, E. D., Shanock, L. R., & Theilgard, N. (2018). Intra-individual response variability as an indicator of insufficient effort responding: Comparison to other indicators and relationships with individual differences. Journal of Business and Psychology, 33(1), 105–121.

Gosling, S. D., Rentfrow, P. J., & Swann, W. B., Jr. (2003). A very brief measure of the Big-Five personality domains. Journal of Research in Personality, 37(6), 504–528.

Huang, J. L., Curran, P. G., Keeney, J., Poposki, E. M., & DeShon, R. P. (2012). Detecting and deterring insufficient effort responding to surveys. Journal of Business and Psychology, 27(1), 99–114.

Johnson, J. A. (2005). Ascertaining the validity of individual protocols from Web-based personality inventories. Journal of Research in Personality, 39(1), 103–129.

Lovibond, S. H., & Lovibond, P. F. (1995). Manual for the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (2nd ed.). Psychology Foundation.

Maniaci, M. R., & Rogge, R. D. (2014). Caring about carelessness: Participant inattention and its effects on research. Journal of Research in Personality, 48, 61–83.

Meade, A. W., & Craig, S. B. (2012). Identifying careless responses in survey data. Psychological Methods, 17(3), 437–455.

See also

  • rwf: the R package behind compute_raw_alpha() on this page

This post first appeared on Scale Validation in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Power Analysis by Simulation in R: How Many People Do I Need?
item.description: Power and sample size by simulation in R: t-tests, ΔR² steps, mediation and multilevel designs, checked against pwr, with sensitivity analysis and APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Power and sample size by simulation in R: t-tests, ΔR² steps, mediation and multilevel designs, checked against pwr, with sensitivity analysis and APA reporting.

The question: how many people do I need?

Before collecting data, every study has to answer one question: how many participants?

  • Too few, and a real effect will often be missed. Worse, the effects that do reach significance in a small study are exaggerated: only the lucky, overestimated ones pass the bar.
  • Too many, and time, money and participants’ goodwill are wasted.

Statistical power is the probability that a study finds an effect (a significant result) when the effect really exists. Four quantities are tied together:

Quantity Symbol Usual choice
Significance level: the chance of a false positive when there is no effect \(\alpha\) .05
Power: the chance of a significant result when the effect is real \(1 - \beta\) .80 or .90
Effect size: how large the effect is assumed to be \(d\), \(r\), \(f^2\), … from theory, earlier studies or the smallest effect that would matter
Sample size \(n\) what we want to find

Fix any three and the fourth follows. For simple analyses there are formulas, which the pwr package implements. For anything more complex (a mediation model, employees nested in teams, missing data, a non-normal outcome) there is one method that always works: simulate the study you plan. This tutorial does both for four common designs, and checks the simulations against the formulas wherever a formula exists.

Code 
library(pwr)        # power formulas: pwr.t.test(), pwr.r.test(), pwr.f2.test()
library(nlme)       # lme(): multilevel models (section 7)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots side by side

1. What power is

Take a study comparing two groups of 64 people each, where the true difference is half a standard deviation (\(d = 0.5\)). We test with a two-sided t-test at \(\alpha = .05\).

If there were no effect, the t statistic would follow the usual t distribution around 0 (the dashed curve below). With a true effect of \(d\), it follows a noncentral t distribution, shifted to the right by the noncentrality parameter

\[\delta = d \sqrt{\frac{n}{2}} = 0.5 \times \sqrt{\frac{64}{2}} = 2.83\]

where \(n\) is the size of each group. We call a result significant when \(|t|\) is beyond the critical value \(t_{crit}\).

Code 
n_demo <- 64; d_demo <- 0.5
df_demo <- 2 * n_demo - 2
ncp_demo <- d_demo * sqrt(n_demo / 2)
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df_demo)
grid_t <- seq(-4, 7.5, length.out = 600)
curves <- rbind(data.frame(t = grid_t, density = dt(grid_t, df_demo), world = "no effect (H0)"),
                data.frame(t = grid_t, density = dt(grid_t, df_demo, ncp = ncp_demo), world = "d = 0.5 (H1)"))
h0 <- subset(curves, world == "no effect (H0)")
h1 <- subset(curves, world == "d = 0.5 (H1)")
ggplot() +
  geom_area(data = subset(h1, t >= t_crit), aes(t, density), fill = "#0082c8", alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_area(data = subset(h1, t < t_crit), aes(t, density), fill = "#95A5A6", alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_area(data = subset(h0, t >= t_crit), aes(t, density), fill = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_area(data = subset(h0, t <= -t_crit), aes(t, density), fill = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(t, density, linetype = world), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-t_crit, t_crit), linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.4, y = 0.25, label = sprintf("power = %.2f", 1 - pt(t_crit, df_demo, ncp_demo)),
           colour = "#0082c8", size = 3.8, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.9, y = 0.25, label = sprintf("beta = %.2f\n(effect missed)", pt(t_crit, df_demo, ncp_demo)),
           colour = "grey30", size = 3.5, hjust = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = -3.1, y = 0.1, label = "alpha / 2\nin each tail", colour = "#E74C3C", size = 3.5) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("no effect (H0)" = "dashed", "d = 0.5 (H1)" = "solid")) +
  labs(title = "Two worlds: the t statistic with no effect and with d = 0.5 (64 per group)",
       x = "t statistic", y = "density", linetype = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  • The red tails are \(\alpha\): the chance of a significant result although nothing is going on (a false positive, type I error). Both tails together make .05.
  • The grey area is \(\beta\): the chance of missing the real effect (a false negative, type II error).
  • The blue area is power, \(1 - \beta\). Here it is 0.80.

A larger effect or a larger sample moves the solid curve further to the right, and the blue area grows. That is all a power analysis does: it finds the \(n\) that moves the curve far enough.

2. The general recipe: simulate the study you plan

A simulation needs no formula. It copies, many times over, exactly what we will do with the real data:

  1. Write down a model for the data, with the effect sizes we assume.
  2. Generate one data set of the planned size from it.
  3. Analyse it exactly as planned, and note whether the result is significant.
  4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 \(R\) times. The power is the share of significant results.
  5. Repeat for other sample sizes, and pick the smallest that gives the power we want.

The two-group study of section 1, written as plainly as possible:

Code 
set.seed(1)
R <- 2000                                         # number of simulated studies
significant <- logical(R)
for (r in 1:R) {
  control   <- rnorm(64, mean = 0,   sd = 1)      # step 2: one data set of the planned size
  treatment <- rnorm(64, mean = 0.5, sd = 1)
  significant[r] <- t.test(treatment, control, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value < 0.05   # step 3
}
power_loop <- mean(significant)                   # step 4: the share of significant results
power_loop
[1] 0.7995

How precise is a simulated power?

Each simulated study is a coin toss that comes up “significant” with probability equal to the power \(p\). After \(R\) tosses, the share of significant results has a Monte Carlo standard error of

\[SE = \sqrt{\frac{p\,(1 - p)}{R}}\]

Code 
mc_se <- function(p, R) sqrt(p * (1 - p) / R)
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^0", "", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # .80 instead of 0.80, for the text
data.frame(replications = c(500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000),
           se_at_power_.80 = round(mc_se(0.8, c(500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000)), 4))
  replications se_at_power_.80
1          500          0.0179
2         1000          0.0126
3         2000          0.0089
4         5000          0.0057
5        10000          0.0040

With 2,000 replications our estimate 0.799 has a standard error of 0.009, so the true power is within about \(\pm\) 0.018 of it. To pin a power of .80 down to \(\pm .01\) (95% confidence) takes \(R = 0.8 \times 0.2 \times (1.96 / 0.01)^2 \approx\) 6,147 replications. A thousand or two is usually enough to choose a sample size; report \(R\) and the standard error with the result.

Faster: many studies at once

A loop is easy to read but slow when there are many sample sizes to try. The same simulation can be written with matrices, one simulated study per row:

Code 
sim_t_power <- function(n, d, R) {
  g1 <- matrix(rnorm(R * n), nrow = R)                 # R studies (rows) of n people (columns)
  g2 <- matrix(rnorm(R * n, mean = d), nrow = R)
  m1 <- rowMeans(g1); m2 <- rowMeans(g2)
  v1 <- rowSums((g1 - m1)^2) / (n - 1); v2 <- rowSums((g2 - m2)^2) / (n - 1)
  t <- (m2 - m1) / sqrt((v1 + v2) / n)                 # Student's t for two groups of equal size
  mean(abs(t) > qt(0.975, df = 2 * n - 2))
}
set.seed(2)
power_fast <- sim_t_power(64, 0.5, 2000)
power_fast
[1] 0.802

3. Two groups: the t-test

For two groups the formula exists. pwr.t.test() solves for whichever argument is left out:

Code 
pwr.t.test(d = 0.5, power = 0.80, sig.level = 0.05)

     Two-sample t test power calculation 
              n = 63.76561
              d = 0.5
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided
NOTE: n is number in *each* group

How to read the output

  • n is the size of each group (the note says so): 63.8, so we round up to 64 per group, 128 in total.
  • d, sig.level and power repeat what we gave. Leave out n and give power to get a sample size; leave out power and give n to get the power of a planned study; leave out d to get the smallest effect a study can detect (section 8).
  • alternative = two.sided: the test looks for a difference in either direction. A one-sided test needs fewer people, but only if the direction was fixed in advance.

The formula behind it is the noncentral t of section 1, which we can write ourselves:

Code 
power_t <- function(n, d, alpha = 0.05) {          # exact power of a two-sided, two-sample t-test
  df <- 2 * n - 2; ncp <- d * sqrt(n / 2); crit <- qt(1 - alpha / 2, df)
  1 - pt(crit, df, ncp) + pt(-crit, df, ncp)
}
round(c(formula = power_t(64, 0.5), simulation_loop = power_loop, simulation_fast = power_fast), 3)
        formula simulation_loop simulation_fast 
          0.801           0.799           0.802

The simulations agree with the formula within their Monte Carlo error.

Power curves

The power of every sample size from 10 to 200 per group, for a small, a medium and a large effect, by formula (lines) and by simulation (points, 1,000 studies each):

Code 
set.seed(3)
curve_n <- seq(10, 200, by = 10)
effects <- c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8)
formula_curves <- expand.grid(n = 10:200, d = effects)
formula_curves$power <- power_t(formula_curves$n, formula_curves$d)
sim_points <- expand.grid(n = curve_n, d = effects)
sim_points$power <- mapply(sim_t_power, sim_points$n, sim_points$d, R = 1000)
ggplot(formula_curves, aes(n, power, colour = factor(d))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = sim_points, size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("0.2" = "#E74C3C", "0.5" = "#f39c12", "0.8" = "#0082c8"),
                      labels = c("d = 0.2", "d = 0.5", "d = 0.8")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Power of a two-group t-test: formula (lines) and simulation (points)",
       x = "people per group", y = "power", colour = NULL)
Code 
n_needed <- sapply(c(0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.8), function(d) ceiling(pwr.t.test(d = d, power = 0.8)$n))
data.frame(d = c(0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.8), per_group = n_needed, total = 2 * n_needed)
    d per_group total
1 0.2       394   788
2 0.3       176   352
3 0.4       100   200
4 0.5        64   128
5 0.8        26    52

Halving the effect roughly quadruples the sample: \(n\) grows with \(1/d^2\). A small effect needs 394 people per group; a large one only 26.

Which effect size to assume?

The answer depends far more on the assumed effect size than on anything else, so this is the decision that matters.

  • Cohen’s “small, medium, large” (\(d\) = 0.2, 0.5, 0.8) were rough guides for when nothing else is known, not facts about any field. Typical effects in psychology are smaller than “medium”: the average effect in a century of social psychology is about \(r = .21\), or \(d \approx 0.43\) (Richard et al., 2003), and in individual-differences research \(r\) = .10, .20 and .30 are better labels for small, typical and large (Gignac & Szodorai, 2016).
  • The smallest effect size of interest is often the best choice: the smallest effect that would matter in practice, or that the theory would care about. If the study can detect that, it can detect anything larger.
  • Effects from earlier studies are a start, but published effects are inflated, because significant results are more likely to be published. Shrink them, or plan for the lower end of their confidence interval.

Why a pilot study’s effect size misleads

It is tempting to run a small pilot study, compute its \(d\), and plan the main study from it. A simulation shows why this goes wrong. The true effect is \(d = 0.4\), which needs 100 people per group. We simulate 5,000 pilot studies of 20 people per group. A researcher abandons the idea if the pilot \(d\) is below 0.1, and otherwise plans the main study for 80% power at the pilot’s \(d\):

Code 
set.seed(4)
n_pilot <- 20; d_true <- 0.4; R_pilot <- 5000
g1 <- matrix(rnorm(R_pilot * n_pilot), R_pilot)
g2 <- matrix(rnorm(R_pilot * n_pilot, mean = d_true), R_pilot)
pooled_sd <- sqrt((apply(g1, 1, var) + apply(g2, 1, var)) / 2)
pilot_d <- (rowMeans(g2) - rowMeans(g1)) / pooled_sd           # the effect size each pilot finds
go_ahead <- pilot_d >= 0.1                                     # pilots that look promising enough
# sample size per group for 80% power at the pilot's d (normal approximation)
planned_n <- ceiling(2 * (qnorm(0.975) + qnorm(0.8))^2 / pilot_d[go_ahead]^2)
achieved_power <- power_t(planned_n, d_true)                   # the power these studies really have
round(c(pilot_d_from = quantile(pilot_d, 0.05), pilot_d_to = quantile(pilot_d, 0.95),
        abandoned = mean(!go_ahead), median_planned_n = median(planned_n),
        median_achieved_power = median(achieved_power),
        share_power_below_.5 = mean(achieved_power < 0.5)), 2)
      pilot_d_from.5%        pilot_d_to.95%             abandoned      median_planned_n median_achieved_power  share_power_below_.5 
                -0.10                  0.95                  0.17                 74.00                  0.68                  0.34
Code 
p_a <- ggplot(data.frame(d = pilot_d), aes(d)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, fill = "#95A5A6", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = d_true, colour = "#E74C3C", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Effect sizes of 5,000 pilots\n(red: the true d = 0.4)", x = "pilot d", y = "pilots")
p_b <- ggplot(data.frame(power = achieved_power), aes(power)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.025, fill = "#0082c8", colour = "white", boundary = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.8, colour = "#E74C3C", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Real power of the main studies\nplanned from them", x = "power", y = "studies")
p_a + p_b

The pilots’ effect sizes run from about -0.10 to 0.95 (90% of them), because 20 people per group estimate \(d\) very roughly. 17% of good ideas are abandoned. Of the studies that go ahead, half have a power below 0.68, and 34% have less than 50%: the pilots that happened to overestimate the effect lead to studies that are too small. Albers and Lakens (2018) call this follow-up bias. Use a pilot to test the procedure, not to estimate the effect size.

4. A correlation, with rwf’s compute_power_r()

How many people are needed to detect a correlation of \(r = .20\), a typical effect in individual-differences research? pwr.r.test() answers with Fisher’s \(z\) approximation:

Code 
pwr.r.test(r = 0.2, power = 0.8)

     approximate correlation power calculation (arctangh transformation) 
              n = 193.0867
              r = 0.2
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

The rwf package draws the whole power curve with compute_power_r(), which calls pwr.r.test() for every sample size from 10 to n. We add simulated points (2,000 studies each) on top:

Code 
sim_r_power <- function(n, rho, R) {
  x <- matrix(rnorm(R * n), R)
  y <- rho * x + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * matrix(rnorm(R * n), R)   # correlation rho with x
  xc <- x - rowMeans(x); yc <- y - rowMeans(y)
  r <- rowSums(xc * yc) / sqrt(rowSums(xc^2) * rowSums(yc^2))
  t <- r * sqrt(n - 2) / sqrt(1 - r^2)                       # the usual test of a correlation
  mean(abs(t) > qt(0.975, n - 2))
}
set.seed(5)
r_points <- data.frame(n = c(50, 100, 150, 194, 250, 300))
r_points$power <- sapply(r_points$n, sim_r_power, rho = 0.2, R = 2000)
power_r <- compute_power_r(n = 300, r = 0.2, sig.level = 0.05, alternative = "two.sided")
power_r$plot +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(data = r_points, colour = "#E74C3C", size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Power to detect r = .20: pwr.r.test() (black) and simulation (red)")
Code 
r194 <- r_points$power[r_points$n == 194]
c(formula_at_194 = power_r$power_table$power[power_r$power_table$n == 194], simulation_at_194 = r194)
   formula_at_194 simulation_at_194 
        0.8018684         0.8025000

With 194 people the power is about .80 by both methods. The formula is an approximation, but a very good one.

5. A ΔR² step in hierarchical regression

In a hierarchical regression we test whether a new predictor adds explained variance over and above others. Suppose four control variables (say age, gender, education and experience) explain 10% of the variance of job performance, and we expect a new test to add \(\Delta R^2 = .02\). The test correlates \(\rho = .3\) with the controls, so part of what it measures they measure too. How many people do we need?

The effect size for the \(F\)-change test is Cohen’s \(f^2\), which divides the added variance by what the full model leaves unexplained:

\[f^2 = \frac{\Delta R^2}{1 - R^2_{full}} = \frac{.02}{1 - .12} = 0.0227\]

Code 
r2_controls <- 0.10; delta_r2 <- 0.02; r2_full <- r2_controls + delta_r2
f2 <- delta_r2 / (1 - r2_full)
k_full <- 5                                         # 4 controls + the new predictor
pwr_f2 <- pwr.f2.test(u = 1, f2 = f2, power = 0.80)
pwr_f2

     Multiple regression power calculation 
              u = 1
              v = 345.2811
             f2 = 0.02272727
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
Code 
n_f2 <- ceiling(pwr_f2$v) + k_full + 1
n_f2
[1] 352

How to read the output

  • u is the numerator degrees of freedom: the number of predictors added in the step (1 here).
  • v is the denominator degrees of freedom, \(n - k_{full} - 1\), where \(k_{full}\) is the number of predictors in the full model. So the sample size is \(n = v + k_{full} + 1\) = 345.3 + 5 + 1, rounded up to 352.
  • f2, sig.level, power: as given. pwr uses the noncentrality \(\lambda = f^2 (u + v + 1)\), about \(f^2 \times n\).

Because \(f^2\) divides by \(1 - R^2_{full}\), the same \(\Delta R^2\) is easier to detect when the controls already explain a lot: there is less noise left.

Code 
data.frame(r2_controls = c(0, 0.10, 0.30, 0.50)) |>
  transform(f2 = round(delta_r2 / (1 - (r2_controls + delta_r2)), 4),
            n = sapply(r2_controls, function(r2c) ceiling(pwr.f2.test(u = 1, f2 = delta_r2 / (1 - r2c - delta_r2),
                                                                      power = 0.8)$v) + k_full + 1))
  r2_controls     f2   n
1         0.0 0.0204 391
2         0.1 0.0227 352
3         0.3 0.0294 273
4         0.5 0.0417 195

The same by simulation

To simulate, we build a population with exactly these properties. The four controls \(X_1, \dots, X_4\) are independent standard normal variables; the new predictor is \(Z = \rho\,\bar X^* + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\,U\), where \(\bar X^* = (X_1 + \dots + X_4)/2\) has variance 1, so the controls explain \(\rho^2\) of \(Z\)’s variance. The outcome is \(y = \beta \sum X_k + \gamma Z + e\) with variance 1. \(Z\)’s unique contribution is \(\gamma^2 (1 - \rho^2) = \Delta R^2\), which fixes \(\gamma\); \(\beta\) is then chosen so that \(R^2_{full} = .12\).

Code 
rho <- 0.3
gamma <- sqrt(delta_r2 / (1 - rho^2))
beta <- uniroot(function(b) 4 * (b + gamma * rho / 2)^2 + gamma^2 * (1 - rho^2) - r2_full, c(0, 1))$root
sim_dr2_power <- function(n, R) {
  mean(replicate(R, {
    X <- matrix(rnorm(n * 4), n)
    Z <- rho * rowSums(X) / 2 + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(n)
    y <- X %*% rep(beta, 4) + gamma * Z + rnorm(n, sd = sqrt(1 - r2_full))
    rss_small <- sum(.lm.fit(cbind(1, X), y)$residuals^2)        # step 1: controls only
    rss_full  <- sum(.lm.fit(cbind(1, X, Z), y)$residuals^2)     # step 2: + the new predictor
    F_change  <- (rss_small - rss_full) / (rss_full / (n - k_full - 1))
    F_change > qf(0.95, 1, n - k_full - 1)
  }))
}
power_f2 <- function(n) { v <- n - k_full - 1; 1 - pf(qf(0.95, 1, v), 1, v, ncp = f2 * (1 + v + 1)) }
set.seed(6)
dr2_points <- data.frame(n = c(100, 200, 300, n_f2, 400, 500))
dr2_points$power <- sapply(dr2_points$n, sim_dr2_power, R = 2000)
dr2_points$formula <- power_f2(dr2_points$n)
round(dr2_points, 3)
    n power formula
1 100 0.332   0.310
2 200 0.557   0.556
3 300 0.727   0.734
4 352 0.806   0.801
5 400 0.852   0.849
6 500 0.918   0.918
Code 
ggplot(data.frame(n = 50:550), aes(n, power_f2(n))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#0082c8") +
  geom_errorbar(data = dr2_points, aes(y = power, ymin = power - 1.96 * mc_se(power, 2000),
                                       ymax = power + 1.96 * mc_se(power, 2000)), width = 8, colour = "#E74C3C") +
  geom_point(data = dr2_points, aes(y = power), colour = "#E74C3C", size = 2.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +

The simulation agrees with the formula. Where they could differ is when the formula’s assumptions fail (skewed outcomes, missing data, predictors with outliers); then only the simulation is right, because we can build any of these into it.

6. Mediation: power for the indirect effect

In a mediation model, \(X\) affects \(M\) (path \(a\)), which affects \(Y\) (path \(b\)), and the indirect effect is \(a \times b\). There is no simple formula for its power, so here simulation is the standard method.

\[M = a X + e_M, \qquad Y = b M + c' X + e_Y\]

We simulate standardised variables (all with variance 1) and no direct effect (\(c' = 0\)). Inside the loop we need a test of \(ab\) that is fast:

  • Joint significance: the indirect effect is significant if both \(a\) and \(b\) are. Simple, and it keeps the false-positive rate correct.
  • Monte Carlo confidence interval (Preacher & Selig, 2012): draw many values of \(a\) and \(b\) from normal distributions with the estimated means and standard errors, multiply them, and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the products. Significant if the interval excludes 0.

The bootstrap confidence interval, the usual choice for real data, refits the model on hundreds of resamples. Inside a simulation that means thousands of studies × a thousand resamples × every sample size, which takes far longer for a similar answer, as we check below.

Code 
sim_mediation <- function(n, a, b, R, draws = 1000) {
  t(replicate(R, {
    x <- rnorm(n)
    m <- a * x + rnorm(n, sd = sqrt(1 - a^2))                    # var(m) = 1
    y <- b * m + rnorm(n, sd = sqrt(1 - b^2))                    # var(y) = 1, c' = 0
    fit_a <- .lm.fit(cbind(1, x), m)
    a_hat <- fit_a$coefficients[2]
    se_a  <- sqrt(sum(fit_a$residuals^2) / (n - 2) / sum((x - mean(x))^2))
    Xb    <- cbind(1, m, x)
    fit_b <- .lm.fit(Xb, y)
    b_hat <- fit_b$coefficients[2]
    se_b  <- sqrt(sum(fit_b$residuals^2) / (n - 3) * solve(crossprod(Xb))[2, 2])
    joint <- abs(a_hat / se_a) > qt(0.975, n - 2) && abs(b_hat / se_b) > qt(0.975, n - 3)
    ab    <- rnorm(draws, a_hat, se_a) * rnorm(draws, b_hat, se_b)   # Monte Carlo draws of a*b
    ci    <- quantile(ab, c(0.025, 0.975))
    c(n = n, joint = joint, monte_carlo = ci[1] > 0 || ci[2] < 0)
  }))
}

Three scenarios, using Cohen’s labels for the paths: two small paths (\(a = b = .14\)), two medium paths (\(a = b = .39\)), and a small \(a\) with a large \(b\) (\(.14\) and \(.59\)). 400 studies per sample size:

Code 
scenarios <- list("a = b = .14 (small, small)"  = list(a = 0.14, b = 0.14, n = c(100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 800)),
                  "a = b = .39 (medium, medium)" = list(a = 0.39, b = 0.39, n = c(30, 45, 60, 75, 90, 120)),

  data.frame(scenario = s, out)
}))
